title: Saisonalität und langfristige Trends des Blattflächenindex in Brandenburg
description: Datengrundlage: Saisonalität und langfristige Trends des Blattflächenindex in Brandenburg Dieser Datensatz enthält die Daten, die den Zeitreihen-Abbildungen und Trendangaben des Abschlussberichts zugrunde liegen: Voit, P., Heistermann, M.: Saisonalität und langfristige Trends des Blattflächenindex in Brandenburg. Abschlussbericht des Teilprojekts „Langfristige Änderungen in der Vegetation und Wechselwirkungen mit dem Landschaftswasserhaushalt“ (TP 1.3) des Vorhabens „Klimafolgen und Anpassung in Brandenburg“. Universität Potsdam, 2026. Verweise auf Abbildungen, Tabellen und Abschnitte beziehen sich auf diesen Bericht. Die Methoden sind dort in Kapitel 3 beschrieben; diese README fasst nur zusammen, was zum Lesen der Dateien nötig ist. Inhalt im Überblick Ordner Inhalt zeitreihen/ entmischter LAI je Landnutzungsklasse, je Produkt und Region gitterzellen/ nicht entmischter LAI je Gitterzelle sowie Lage, Region und CORINE-Flächenanteile der Zellen trends/ Jahrestrends, Monatstrends und mittlerer Jahresgang je Produkt, Zeitraum und Region; Bruchpunkttests; Landesmittel produktvergleich/ Trends der drei Produkte nebeneinander, mit Produktmittel phaenologie/ DWD-Beobachtungen der Waldkiefer (Maitrieb), daraus gebildete Jahresreihen und Vergleich mit dem Beginn der Vegetationsperiode (SOS) aus dem LAI 1. Allgemeine Konventionen Dateiformat. Alle Dateien sind CSV-Dateien (UTF-8) mit Semikolon als Trennzeichen und Punkt als Dezimaltrennzeichen. Datumsangaben im Format JJJJ-MM-TT. Leere Felder bedeuten: kein Wert. Produkte (Ordner- und Dateinamen): Kürzel Produkt Zeitraum zeitliche Auflösung Gitterzellen in Brandenburg gimms-lai4g GIMMS LAI4g (Cao et al., 2023a, b) 1982–2020 halbmonatlich (1. und 15. des Monats) 516 hiq-lai HiQ-LAI (Yan et al., 2023, 2024) 2000–2022 8 Tage 1876 si-lai-fpar SI LAI/FPAR (Pu et al., 2023, 2024) 2000–2022 8 Tage 1502 Zeiträume. Für GIMMS LAI4g werden drei Zeiträume ausgewertet: die gesamte Reihe 1982–2020, der rekonstruierte Abschnitt 1982–2003 und der beobachtete Abschnitt 2004–2020. Der Datensatz ist an der Bruchstelle 2004 inkonsistent (Abschnitt 4.1 und 5.1 des Berichts). Trends über die gesamte Reihe 1982–2020 und für den rekonstruierten Abschnitt 1982–2003 sind deshalb nicht belastbar und nur zum Vergleich enthalten. HiQ-LAI und SI LAI/FPAR werden über ihre gesamte Reihe 2000–2022 ausgewertet. Regionen (Ordner- und Dateinamen): brandenburg = gesamtes Untersuchungsgebiet, nord = Nordbrandenburg, sued = Südbrandenburg. Die Grenze ist die Nordkante der Zellreihe, in der Kyritz liegt; jede Zelle wird nach der Lage ihres Mittelpunkts zugeordnet (Abschnitt 3.1, Abbildung 2). Berlin gehört nicht zum Untersuchungsgebiet. Ausgewertet sind nur Zellen, die zu mindestens 75 % in Brandenburg liegen. Landnutzungsklassen. Die Spalten tragen englische Kurznamen: Spalte Klasse im Bericht CLC-Codes (Tabelle 7) pineforest Nadelwald (in Brandenburg überwiegend Kiefer) 312 otherforest sonstiger Wald 141, 311, 313, 324 cropland Acker 211, 222, 242, 243 grassland Grünland 231, 321, 322, 411 other Restklasse (bebaute Flächen, Gewässer, Abbau, Sand u. a.) übrige Codes Die Restklasse wird im Bericht nicht ausgewertet; ihr LAI ist in der Entmischung auf 0–0,1 begrenzt. Einheiten. LAI in m²/m². Sen-Steigungen (sen_slope, *_slope) in m²/m² pro Jahr; der Bericht nennt sie teils zusätzlich pro Dekade (× 10). Phänologische Termine als Tag im Jahr (DOY), deren Trends in Tagen pro Jahr. Winterzeitraum. Werte der Kompositen mit Beginn zwischen 15. November und 25. Januar sind in allen Produkten und Zeiträumen entfernt (Abschnitt 2.6 des Berichts; Ursache: unzuverlässige Winterwerte der LAI-Produkte). Dezember und Januar haben daher keine Monatstrends; der November beruht bei GIMMS LAI4g nur auf seiner ersten Hälfte. Einzige Ausnahme sind die Dateien mit dem Zusatz _ganzjahr (siehe unten). Signifikanz (significance, *_sig): *** p < 0,001, ** p < 0,01, * p < 0,05, ns nicht signifikant, n/a nicht berechnet (zu wenige Werte). 2. zeitreihen/ – entmischter LAI je Landnutzungsklasse Datei Inhalt im Bericht gimms-lai4g/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv GIMMS LAI4g, 1982–2020, halbmonatlich, ohne Winterzeitraum Abb. 3, 5, 9, 12–17; Grundlage aller GIMMS-Trends gimms-lai4g/{brandenburg,nord,sued}_ganzjahr.csv wie oben, aber mit Winterzeitraum Abb. 8 (mittlerer Jahresgang) hiq-lai/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv HiQ-LAI, 2000–2022, 8 Tage, ohne Winterzeitraum Grundlage der HiQ-Trends si-lai-fpar/{brandenburg,nord,sued}.csv SI LAI/FPAR, 2000–2022, 8 Tage, ohne Winterzeitraum Grundlage der SI-Trends Spalten: datetime (Beginn des Kompositums), dann je Klasse der entmischte LAI (pineforest, grassland, otherforest, cropland, other). Entmischung (Abschnitt 3.2): Für jeden Zeitschritt wird der LAI aller Gitterzellen der Region als flächengewichtete Mischung der Klassen-LAI modelliert (Anteile aus CORINE Land Cover mit Change-Layern, siehe gitterzellen/). Die Klassen-LAI werden per beschränkter Kleinste-Quadrate-Schätzung bestimmt. Grenzen: Nadelwald 1–5, sonstiger Wald 0–8, Acker 0–5, Grünland 0–5, Restklasse 0–0,1. Werte genau an einer Grenze (z. B. Nadelwald = 1,0 bei HiQ-LAI) sind möglich. Sehr kleine Werte wie 5e-324 sind numerisch null. 3. gitterzellen/ – nicht entmischte Werte und Zellbeschreibung Datei Inhalt im Bericht <produkt>_lai_je_zelle.csv LAI je Gitterzelle und Zeitschritt, wie er in die Entmischung eingeht Abb. 4, Tabelle 3, Landesmittel (Tab. 4) <produkt>_zellen.csv Lage, Region und Landnutzungsanteile je Zelle Abb. 2 (GIMMS) <produkt>_lai_je_zelle.csv: Spalte datetime, danach eine Spalte je Zelle; der Spaltenname ist die cell_id. Werte auf drei Nachkommastellen. Aufbereitung wie im Bericht (Abschnitt 3.1): Skalierung, Füllwerte entfernt, bei HiQ-LAI Qualitätsfilter angewendet, Winterzeitraum entfernt. Bei HiQ-LAI enthalten 77 Zellen nach dem Qualitätsfilter keinen gültigen Wert. <produkt>_zellen.csv: Spalte Bedeutung cell_id Zellnummer (= Spaltenname in _lai_je_zelle.csv) lon, lat Zellmittelpunkt in Grad (WGS 84), berechnet im Gitter ETRS89/UTM 33N (EPSG:25833) region nord oder sued frac_<klasse>_<jahr> Flächenanteil der Klasse an der Zelle für die CORINE-Bezugsjahre 1990, 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018 Die Flächenanteile wurden aus CORINE Land Cover 1990 und den Change-Layern 1990–2000 bis 2012–2018 abgeleitet (Abschnitt 2 „Landbedeckung“ des Berichts). Für die Jahre zwischen zwei Bezugsjahren werden sie in der Entmischung linear interpoliert. GIMMS LAI4g: 113 Zellen Nord, 403 Süd. HiQ-LAI: 439 Nord, 1437 Süd. SI LAI/FPAR: 334 Nord, 1168 Süd. 4. trends/ – Trends, Bruchpunkte, mittlerer Jahresgang Aufbau: trends/<produkt>/<zeitraum>/<region>/<datei>.csv Produkt Zeiträume gimms-lai4g 1982-2020, 1982-2003, 2004-2020 hiq-lai 2000-2022 si-lai-fpar 2000-2022 4.1 jahrestrends.csv – Trend je Landnutzungsklasse Tabellen 2, 4, 5, 9; Abbildungen 3, 5, 6, 7, 19. Methode (Abschnitt 3.3): Von der entmischten Reihe wird der mittlere Jahresgang abgezogen (Anomalien je Zeitschritt). Darauf werden Mann-Kendall-Test mit Autokorrelationskorrektur nach Hamed und Rao (1998) und Sen-Steigung angewendet. Zusätzlich ein Pettitt-Test auf einen Bruchpunkt im Mittelwert. Spalte Bedeutung landuse Landnutzungsklasse n_obs Anzahl der Zeitschritte mit Wert mk_trend Richtung (increasing, decreasing, no trend) sen_slope Sen-Steigung, m²/m² pro Jahr mk_p p-Wert Mann-Kendall significance Signifikanzstufe mk_method Testvariante (hamed_rao) breakpoint_date, pettitt_p wahrscheinlichster Bruchpunkt nach Pettitt und sein p-Wert 4.2 monatstrends.csv – Trend je Kalendermonat und Klasse Abbildungen 9, 10, 15–18; Tabelle 8. Methode: Je Jahr und Kalendermonat ein Wert (Mittel der Werte des Monats), darauf Mann-Kendall-Test ohne Autokorrelationskorrektur (mk_method = original) und Sen-Steigung. Spalten wie in jahrestrends.csv, zusätzlich month (1–12). Dezember und Januar: insufficient_data (Winterzeitraum). 4.3 jahresgang.csv – mittlerer Jahresgang Je Kalendermonat das Mittel (<klasse>_mean) und die Standardabweichung zwischen den Jahren (<klasse>_std) des entmischten LAI; month, month_name. Ohne Winterzeitraum, daher Dezember und Januar leer. gimms-lai4g/2004-2020/brandenburg/jahresgang_ganzjahr.csv: dasselbe mit Winterzeitraum – das ist die Grundlage von Abbildung 8 (Nutzerentscheidung: der mittlere Jahresgang wird mit allen Monaten gezeigt, nur die Trends ohne Winterzeitraum). 4.4 <produkt>/bruchpunkt_streuung.csv – Bruchpunkt in der Streuung Pettitt-Test auf den Betrag der Anomalien (Maß für die Streuung) über die gesamte Reihe, je Region (all = Brandenburg, north, south) und Klasse. Bei GIMMS LAI4g liegt der Bruchpunkt in Brandenburg für Nadelwald und Grünland im Frühjahr 2004, für Acker im Frühjahr 2005 (Bruchstelle 2004, Abschnitt 4.1); für sonstigen Wald 1998. Bei HiQ-LAI und SI LAI/FPAR gibt es keinen systematischen Bruchpunkt über alle Klassen. Tabelle 3 (Streuung vor/nach 2004) ist aus gitterzellen/gimms-lai4g_lai_je_zelle.csv berechnet (Gebietsmittel über alle Zellen bzw. Standardabweichung der Anomalien je Zelle). 4.5 landesmittel.csv – Trend des Landesmittels Zeile „Landesmittel“ in Tabelle 4. Mittel über alle Gitterzellen (nicht entmischt), mittlerer Jahresgang abgezogen, Mann-Kendall mit Hamed-Rao-Korrektur. Spalte Bedeutung produkt, zeitraum, zellen Produkt, Zeitraum, Anzahl Zellen sen_pro_jahr, sen_pro_dekade Sen-Steigung in m²/m² pro Jahr bzw. pro Dekade p p-Wert 5. produktvergleich/ – drei Produkte nebeneinander produktvergleich/<region>/jahrestrends.csv (Tabellen 4, 5; Abbildungen 6, 7) und produktvergleich/<region>/monatstrends.csv (Tabelle 8). title: Global Snow-free Leaf Area Index Dataset for Earth System Modeling – Year 1998
description: The snow-free Leaf Area Index (LAI) dataset is a global monthly LAI product developed for land surface and earth system modeling. It covers the period from 1985 to 2020 at 500 m spatial resolution and aims to constrain the underestimation of LAI in snow-covered regions caused by snow contamination. The dataset was generated by integrating reprocessed MODIS Collection 6.1 LAI and GIMMS LAI4g products with plant functional type (PFT) information. Snow-affected areas were identified using satellite-based observations, and LAI was corrected at the PFT level using leaf lifespan constraints derived from the TRY plant trait database. The resulting snow-free LAI better represents the phenology of evergreen vegetation and is intended to support studies of vegetation–snow interactions, land surface processes, and earth system modeling. The dataset provides monthly LAI and SAI at 500 m spatial resolution globally, distributed as NetCDF-4 format files. Each file covers a 5° × 5° geographic region containing 1200 × 1200 pixels (0.00416667° or 15 arc-seconds per pixel) in the WGS84 coordinate system. The global land surface is divided into 1,447 regional tiles, with files named according to the convention RG_LatN_LonW_LatS_LonE.LSAI500m.YYYY.nc, where the latitude and longitude bounds define the tile coverage and YYYY indicates the year. Each file contains four primary data variables: MONTHLY_LC_LAI and MONTHLY_LC_SAI representing 500 m grid LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 1200 lat × 1200 lon), and MONTHLY_PFT_LAI and MONTHLY_PFT_SAI providing PFT LAI and SAI values with dimensions (12 months × 16 PFTs × 1200 lat × 1200 lon). Grid LAI (SAI) and PFT LAI (SAI) are both available for user selection according to research demands. The grid LAI (SAI) is calculated as the area-weighted average of PFT LAI (SAI). All LAI and SAI values are stored as unsigned byte integers with a scale factor of 0.1 and units of m2/m2, requiring multiplication by 0.1 to obtain physical values. The 16 plant functional types include various tree, shrub, grass, and crop categories ranging from tropical to boreal biomes. Coordinate variables (lat, lon, pft, mon) are included with appropriate metadata.

title: Derived Optimal Linear Combination Evapotranspiration - DOLCE
description: DOLCE V3.0 is an observationally constrained hybrid Evapotranspiration (ET) dataset with uncertainty estimates. It is derived by merging four global ET datasets: - ERA5-land (Muñoz S. J., 2019) - FLUXCOM METEO+RS (Jung et al., 2019) - GLEAM v3.5a and GLEAM v3.5b (Martens B. et al., 2017). The combination of these parent datasets is based on their performance against flux tower ET, and accounts for their error dependency. The weights assigned to the parent datasets vary by seasons (Dec-May / Jun-Nov) and climate regimes based on a simplified climate regime map. DOLCE V3.0 provides time-variant estimates of its uncertainty errors. Similar to DOLCE V2.1, DOLCE V3.0 is monthly, has 0.25-degree spatial resolution, available over 1980 - 2018, and covers the global land. DOLCE V3.0 is suitable for time-series and trends analysis. The reduced number of participating datasets compared to previous versions is to ensure temporal consistency throughout the covered time period. In comparison, DOLCE V2.1, which was derived from the combination of 11 global datasets, is suitable for climatological analysis, and is less biased against flux tower observations than DOLCE V3.0. However, temporal inconsistencies around the years 2001 and 2016 were detected in DOLCE V2.1 over the tropics. These inconsistencies result from the different lengths of records of the parent datasets. We, therefore, advise the user to select an appropriate dataset for their research based on the application. title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data
description: This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP. From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it. The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1); • The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp); • Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted); • Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution. NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts. A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code. Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010.

title: Drought risk of global terrestrial gross primary productivity in recent 40 years detected by a remote sensing-driven process model
description: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the largest flux in the global terrestrial carbon cycle and affected by multiple factors. In recent decades, drought has significantly impacted global terrestrial GPP and been projected to occur with increasing frequency and intensity. However, the drought risk of global terrestrial GPP has not been well investigated. In this study, global terrestrial GPP over the period from 1981 to 2016 was simulated with the process-based Boreal Ecosystem Productivity Simulator (BEPS) model. Then, the drought risk of terrestrial GPP was quantified as the product of frequency of drought and reduction of GPP caused by drought, which were determined using the standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI). During the study period, the drought risk of terrestrial GPP exhibited detectable spatial heterogeneity, high in southeastern United States, most of South America, southern Europe, central and eastern Africa, eastern and southeastern Asia, and eastern Australia. In these regions, the maximum reduction of GPP might be above 30% in drought years relative to that in normal years. The drought risk of GPP was low at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, in which terrestrial GPP increased slightly in drought years. The spatial pattern of the drought risk of GPP simulated by the BEPS model was close to that of FLUXCOM GPP, which was scaled from tower observations with a machine learning algorithm forced by remote sensing and meteorological data. This study advances our understanding on the impact of drought on terrestrial GPP over the globe.

title: Global Observationally-Based Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics (GOLAM)
description: The Global Observationally-Based Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics (GOLAM) provide a comprehensive representation of land-atmosphere (L-A) coupling indices based on observationally derived (mainly satellite-based) gridded datasets. This dataset includes L-A coupling indices such as Pearson correlation coefficients and terrestrial coupling indices between daily soil moisture (SM) and surface heat fluxes, including sensible heat flux (H), evaporation (E), and evaporative fraction (EF), as well as SM memory. These indices are designed to account for random observational errors present in satellite SM measurements by employing a Markovian framework. The global patterns of surface and sub-surface SM regimes and SM-EF indicators, such as wilting point, critical SM, saturated EF, and SM-EF slope, are also quantified through segmented regression analysis. Multiple SM and flux data products are used to develop these datasets, including: two SM satellite datasets: SMAP and ESA CCI, a machine learning SM dataset: SoMo, and three surface heat flux datasets: GLEAM, CAMELE, and FluxCom-X-BASE. For consistency, the Land-Atmosphere Coupling Metrics datasets are provided at a spatial resolution of 0.25˚*0.25˚; however, the SMAP-GLEAM and SMAP-only combinations are available at both 0.1˚*0.1˚ and 0.25˚*0.25˚. The temporal coverage of these metrics depends on the input datasets and is provided across four different seasons: June-August (JJA), September-November (SON), December-February (DJF), and March-May (MAM), as well as composited warm seasons across three regions: May through September (MJJAS) for 23˚N-60˚N, November through March (NDJFM) for 23˚S-60˚S, and all months for 23˚S-23˚N. However, SM regimes are only calculated during warm seasons, depending on the latitude bands. The source code for generating GOLAM is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17702299.

title: Impacts of Land Use Change and atmospheric CO2 on Gross Primary Productivity (GPP), evaporation and climate in Southern Amazon (Open)
description: This work was carried out in the scope and with the support of the project: Climate Services Through Knowledge Co-Production: A Euro-South American Initiative for Strengthening Societal Adaptation Response to Extreme Events (CLIMAX). The project consortium includes the following institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique CNRS/Instituto Franco-Argentino sobre Estudios de Clima y sus Impactos (UMI-IFAECI) (Argentina-France); General Coordination of Earth Sciences /National Institute for Space Research (INPE) (Brazil); Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD)/ Unité Mixte de Recherche (UMR 245) (France); Le Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l'Environnement (LSCE) (France); Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) (Germany); Technical University of Munich (TUM) (Germany) and Wageningen University and Research (WUR) Netherlands). The project is sponsored by the Collaborative Research Action (CRA) on “Climate Predictability and Inter-Regional Linkages” of the Belmont Forum, launched in 2015. Climate variability patterns linking the South American Monsoon region, including Amazonia, with southeastern South America influence climate extremes and impact several societal sectors. More than 200 million people live in the study region, which is also one of the largest agricultural production regions of the world and home to the world’s second largest hydroelectric power plant. The objectives of CLIMAX include better understanding the combined role of remote and local drivers on South American climate variability from sub-seasonal to decadal timescales, and its impact on the occurrence and intensity of extreme events. Special focus is given to an improved understanding of the effects of land use changes from the Amazon to the subtropics and their impact on climate. EXPERIMENT DESIGN We used four models that are classified as Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) (Prentice et al., 2007; Rezende et al., 2015): Integrated Model of Land Surface Processes (INLAND) (Tourigny, 2014); Lund-Potsdam-Jena managed Land model version 4 (LPJmL4) (Schaphoff et al., 2018), Lund-Potsdam-Jena General Ecosystem Simulator (LPJ-GUESS) (Smith et al. 2001, Hickler et al., 2012), and Organising Carbon and Hydrology In Dynamic Ecosystems model (ORCHIDEE) (Krinner et al., 2005). We used three forcings with climate data (GLDAS, GSWP3, and WATCH+WFDEI), Land Use Change (LUC) data and validation data (FLUXCOM (Remote sensor+meteorological data+artificial neural network approach), FLUXCOM (eddy covariance), MODIS (Light Use Efficiency), GLEAM, and TerraClimate (Rezende et al., 2022). We conducted two sets of simulation experiments with different values of CO2: 1) increasing CO2 from the pre-industrial period to 2010 named historical CO2 (hist CO2); 2) constant concentration of 278 ppm of (pre-industrial) atmospheric CO2 named constant CO2 (const CO2). We ran both CO2 experiments under Land Use Change (LUC) and Potential Natural Vegetation (PNV) conditions. All combinations of CO2 and land use change resulted in four sets of simulation experiments per climate input: 1. LUC historical CO2; 2. LUC constant CO2; 3. PNV historical CO2; 4. PNV constant CO2 (Rezende et al., 2022). 2. DATA DESCRIPTION The complete description of the data, including the climate forcing, LUC, the validation datasets, methodology, simulations, discussion and conclusion is in Rezende et al. (2022). title: Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code
description: # Localizing and repairing structural deficits of a conceptual hydrological model with multi-source observations: data and code ## Overview This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce the analysis of structural deficits in the conceptual rainfall-runoff model SIMHYD. The method works as follows: - A differentiable version of SIMHYD carries correction slots of identical structure and capacity on eight fluxes (S1–S8). - Forcing errors and observation errors are modeled separately from structural errors. - A deficit is localized by comparing competing single-slot hypotheses with a significance test. The comparison uses streamflow and, where available, soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET) and snow water equivalent (SWE). - After localization, only the localized slots are repaired, and the repair is evaluated with variables not used in training. The package covers two applications: 1. **Synthetic experiments.** Ten types of implanted structural deficits (D1–D9) and compound deficits (C1–C3) are tested, together with a no-deficit control (D0). Two independently generated truth sets are used (realizations r0 and r1), with eight observation combinations, two observation-quality levels and three types of input error. 2. **Application to 156 CAMELS basins** in the conterminous United States. Training uses streamflow, ESA CCI soil moisture, ERA5-Land or GLEAM evaporation, and UA SWE. Independent evaluation uses FLUXCOM-X-BASE ET and MODIS NDVI. All results shown in the figures and tables of the associated article can be recomputed from the files in `data/results/`. The 12 figure scripts in `code/figs/` reproduce the article figures pixel for pixel from this package. ## Package structure ``` structural-deficit-localization/ ├── README.md this file ├── LICENSE licenses of the code and the data ├── code/ Python code (see code/README.md) │ ├── README.md │ ├── LICENSE MIT License │ ├── requirements.txt │ ├── paths.py locations of the data folders │ ├── models/ differentiable SIMHYD, truth models, correction slots │ ├── data/ readers for CAMELS, Daymet and the gridded observation products │ ├── synth/ generator of the synthetic truth and observations │ ├── train/ losses and the localization model / trainer │ ├── scripts/ experiment runners │ ├── eval/ analyses that produce the summary tables │ ├── figs/ figure scripts │ └── tests/ unit tests └── data/ input data and experiment outputs (see data/README.md) ├── README.md ├── LICENSE CC BY 4.0, with the conditions for third-party data ├── basins/ list of the 156 basins with their groups ├── camels/ CAMELS attributes, basin boundaries, basin forcing, Daymet forcing ├── basin_observations/ basin means of the gridded observation products ├── model_input/ synthetic and real data sets read by the experiments └── results/ outputs of all experiments and summary tables ``` ## Quick start All commands are run from the `code/` folder. The code was tested with Python 3.9 on Windows 10; the package versions are listed in `code/requirements.txt`. ``` cd code pip install -r requirements.txt python -m unittest discover -s tests -t . # 37 tests, about 3 minutes on a CPU python -m figs.fig2_synthetic_success # writes figures/fig2_synthetic_success.png/.pdf ``` The figure scripts `figs.fig1_schematic` to `figs.fig9_ndvi` and `figs.figS1_precip_prior` to `figs.figS3_phenology_maps` read only `data/` and write to a new `figures/` folder at the package root. The map figures use cartopy, which downloads the Natural Earth 1:50m boundaries on first use. To rerun the experiments themselves, see `code/README.md`. The full set of experiments takes several days on a desktop computer with a 16-core CPU and one 12 GB GPU; a single experiment tag takes between about one hour and one day. A GPU is optional. ## Source data The basin-level data in `data/` were derived from the following public data sets. Users of these data should follow the terms of use of the original providers. | Data set | Use in this package | Provider and link | |---|---|---| | CAMELS-US time series and attributes | streamflow, forcing (P, T, PET), basin attributes, basin boundaries, Daymet basin forcing | NCAR, https://doi.org/10.5065/D6MW2F4D and https://doi.org/10.5065/D6G73C3Q | | ESA CCI Soil Moisture v09.2 COMBINED | soil moisture observations | CEDA, https://doi.org/10.5285/d4e66299f5054129b8076fb7502949e1 | | ERA5-Land | total evaporation and potential evaporation | Copernicus Climate Data Store, https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.e2161bac | | GLEAM v4.3a | actual and potential evaporation | https://www.gleam.eu | | UA SWE (NSIDC-0719) | snow water equivalent | NSIDC, https://doi.org/10.5067/0GGPB220EX6A | | FLUXCOM-X-BASE | ET for independent evaluation | ICOS Carbon Portal, https://doi.org/10.18160/5NZG-JMJE | | FLUXCOM RS ensemble | ET, additional comparison only | https://www.fluxcom.org | | MOD13C1 v006 NDVI | independent evaluation of the phenology formulation | NASA LP DAAC, https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13C1.006 | The raw gridded products are not included. The scripts in `code/data/` that compute the basin means from the raw files are included; see `code/README.md`. ## License The code in `code/` is released under the MIT License (`code/LICENSE`). The data produced in this work are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (`data/LICENSE`). These are the synthetic data sets, the experiment outputs and summaries, and the basin list. The basin-level data derived from the third-party products listed above remain subject to the terms of use of their original providers. ## Contact Jun Guo, prof_guojun@hust.edu.cn

title: Regional datasets of long-term and coarse resolution irrigation estimates from space
description: Description The products are experimental datasets of long-term (approximately 20 years) Irrigation Water Use at 0.25° resolution. They cover four regions: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro River Basin in north-eastern Spain, the Murray-Darling Basin in south-eastern Australia, and India. These datasets are the outcome of the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative Anthropogenic Water Use (CCI-AWU) precursor project (project link). They were produced using three different methods: SM-based (Soil-Moisture-based) Inversion, SM-based Delta, and Model-Observation Integration, which is based on the Noah-Multiparameterization model. The SM-based Inversion method was used to produce five datasets for the four regions, each using a different SM product as input. These include ESA CCI Combined, ESA CCI Passive, ASCAT (Advanced Scatterometer), SMOS (Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity), and SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive). The SM-based Delta method was used to produce six datasets for the four regions, each combining different SM and evapotranspiration (ET) products as input. The combinations include ESA CCI Combined SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Active SM & FLUXCOM ET, ESA CCI Combined SM & SSEBOP ET, ESA CCI Passive SM & SSEBOP ET, and ESA CCI Active SM & SSEBOP ET. The Model-Observation Integration method was applied to the CONUS and Murray-Darling Basin regions, producing three datasets using different irrigated surface maps as input. These maps include the Landsat-Derived Global Rainfed and Irrigated-Cropland Product (referred to as "Landsat", the Relative Bias Approach (referred to as "Method1"), and the Multi-Resolution Analysis Approach (referred to as "Method2"). The irrigation products are delivered with monthly temporal aggregation. Acknowledgements: The datasets were developed as part of the ESA CCI-AWU precursor project (contract no. 4000142449/23/I-NB).

description: This repository contains data sets that were submitted to and analysed in the ocean branch of phase two of the REgional Carbon Cycle Assessment and Processes (RECCAP2-ocean) project. Protocols defining the criteria for data set submissions to RECCAP2-ocean are available through the project website: https://reccap2-ocean.github.io/protocols/ A detailed description of the submitted data sets is provided in three files contained in the supplementary.tar file. All originally submitted files were unpacked, compressed, and repacked into tar files before submission to Zenodo. title: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - Models and data sets for the ocean sink estimate in the Global Carbon Budget
description: Global Carbon Budget Ocean - 2026 Release This dataset provides surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs), surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products) and the ocean inverse model OCIM (interior ocean observationally-constrained estimate). Types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series (2) one file per GOBM and simulation (A, B) with gridded fields (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations (4) the gridded file of the natural steady state fluxes from simulation B of six GOBMs that exclude riverine fluxes and have a globally-integrated natural steady state CO2 flux within ± 0.2 GtC yr-1. This data is used to subtract the natural steady state fluxes from the fCO2-products in regional anaylses (Figures 14 and 15) (5) A file for the gridded CO2 fluxes and one file for the global time-series of the ocean inverse model OCIM (simulations C and B) that is used as an observationally-constrained interior ocean data-product in GCB. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2026, are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 spreadsheet (https://globalcarbonbudget.org/datahub/). The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2026 paper, the river flux adjustment needs to be added and an adjustment for the natural steady state fluxes needs to be subtracted from the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (River flux adjustment: North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2026 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Three of the ten fCO2-products (UExP-FFN-U, JMA-MLR and AOML-ET) include a temperature adjustment to correct the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files. fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude (3) One file 'GCB2026_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. (4) One file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_1959_2025.nc) that contains the gridded field and one file (GCB2026_OCIM-48L_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2025.nc) that contains the global time-series of CO2 fluxes of OCIM for simulations C and B. Further data availability: Access and download the additional data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ In addition to the zenodo deposit, the complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. In addition to the data described above, this Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination: The GCB2026-OCEAN data sets were contributed by international research groups. The creators listed in this record include the GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators and a representative of each contributing data set. GCB2026-OCEAN coordinators: Judith Hauck and Peter Landschützer with support from Simone Le Chevère and Alizée Roobaert. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the ocean carbon sink. GCB2026-OCEAN dataset: Hauck et al. description: version update 06 July 2026: corrected erroneous area data in OceanSODA fCO2-product. -- Surface ocean fugacity of CO2 (fCO2) and air-sea CO2 flux data from individual Global Ocean Biogeochemistry Models (GOBMs) and surface ocean fCO2-based data-products (fCO2-products). There are three types of files: (1) one file per fCO2-product with gridded fields and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series, (2) one file per GOBM and simulation with gridded fields, and (3) one file with the globally and regionally-integrated time-series for the GOBMs for all four simulations. Note: These provided gridded outputs from fCO2-based data-products and GOBMs are regridded datasets, without adjustments. The best estimates of the annual global ocean carbon sink, based on the native grids of fCO2-products and GOBMs and with the adjustments described in the Global Carbon Budget 2025 (https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025), are available in the Global Carbon Budget 2025 spreadsheet. The regionally-integrated time-series are as provided by the contributing groups, i.e. integrated from their native grids. In order to reproduce Figure 14 of the Global Carbon Budget 2024 paper (https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025), the river flux adjustment needs to be added to the CO2 flux estimated from the fCO2-products (North: 0.14 GtC yr-1, Tropics: 0.42 GtC yr-1, South: 0.09 GtC yr-1, see GCB 2025 paper). The sum of the regional fluxes may differ from the global estimates as reported in the GCB spreadsheet, because some adjustments were applied only for global fluxes. Two of the 9 fCO2-producst (i.e. JMA-MLR and UExP-FNN-U) include a temperature adjustment to correct the the original fCO2 measurements from measurement depth to the surface layer at the air-sea interface following Ford et al (2025, https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.15656803). Model simulations: Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) Simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) Simulation C ('CO2 effect', forced by observed atmospheric CO2, but excludes climate change and variability) Simulation D ('climate effect on natural carbon cycle', constant CO2, but includes climate change and variability) What is in the files? (1) The files for the fCO2-based data-products contain the following variables (temporal resolution: monthly): fgco2_reg: Regionally integrated air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), monthly, for regions: global, north, tropics, south fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude area: Area per pixel, dimensions: latitude, longitude area_reg: Total surface ocean area covered by native grid, for global, north, tropics, south (2) The files for the GOBMs contain the following fields. Temporal resolution: monthly. Simulation A ('contemporary simulation', including effects of rising CO2, climate change and variability) and simulation B ('control simulation', constant CO2, no climate change and variability) are saved in separate files. fgco2: Flux density of the total air-sea CO2 flux (positive downward), dimensions: time, latitude, longitude sfco2: Surface ocean fCO2, dimensions: time, latitude, longitude (3) One file 'GCB2025_GOBMs_fgco2_timeseries_1959_2024.nc' with the globally and regionally-integrated CO2 flux time-series for all individual GOBMs,for simulations A, B, C and D. We also report an adjusted global time-series of simulation A that accounts for model drift (Aadj). It does not account for the 10% upscaling that is further applied for the calculation of SOCEAN. Regions: North, tropics, south. Temporal resolution: annual. Fair data use statement: The data and model output provided on this site are freely available and were furnished by individual scientists who encourage their use. Citation: Please cite the Global Carbon Budget 2025 (Friedlingstein et al., 2025, ESSD, https://doi.org/10.18160/GCP-2025) for all data. In addition, please also cite the corresponding original reference for each dataset that has been used - see Table 4 in Global Carbon Budget 2025 for references of all the individual Global Ocean Biogeochemical Models and fCO2-based data-products. Further, for an overview of the Global Ocean Biogeochemical Model output, you may find it useful to cite Hauck et al. (2020, Frontiers, doi:10.3389/fmars.2020.571720). Acknowledgement: Please add the following text in the acknowledgement of your paper: "We acknowledge the Global Carbon Project, which is responsible for the Global Carbon Budget and we thank the ocean modeling and fCO2-mapping groups for producing and making available their model and fCO2-product output." Co-authorship: An invitation of co-authorship to the contributing groups is encouraged if these data are the central data set of the publication. Besides the surface fCO2 and air-sea CO2 flux data that is made available open access, we make additional 3D output from the Global Ocean Biogeochemical models (GCB-ocean) available upon request and with its own data policy.

title: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget
description: TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget — 2026 Release This dataset provides gridded terrestrial biosphere model output from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional Scale Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, contributing to the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026). TRENDY is an international model intercomparison project that brings together simulations from dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) to investigate the global terrestrial carbon cycle and its response to environmental change, including atmospheric CO₂, climate variability and land-use change. This release contains the final gridded model output submitted for GCB2026. The simulations support the assessment of the global land carbon sink and analyses of terrestrial carbon fluxes, stocks and their variability. Experimental design and simulations The TRENDY-GCB2026 protocol comprises seven simulations (S0–S6) designed to investigate the effects of changing atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, nitrogen deposition, climate and land use on the terrestrial carbon cycle. Simulations S4–S6 are introduced for the first time in GCB2026. The simulations differ in which environmental drivers vary historically and which are held at pre-industrial conditions: Simulation CO₂ / N deposition Climate Land use / N fertilisation S0 Fixed Fixed Fixed S1 Transient Fixed Fixed S2 Transient Transient Fixed S3 Transient Transient Transient S4 Fixed Fixed Transient S5 Transient Fixed Transient S6 Fixed Transient Transient Fixed conditions correspond to pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ concentrations (year 1700), repeated early 20th-century climate (1901–1920), and pre-industrial land cover, wood harvest and nitrogen inputs, as applicable. Transient conditions follow historical changes in the corresponding drivers. Changes introduced in GCB2026 In previous Global Carbon Budgets, the land carbon sink (SLAND) was estimated primarily from S2, which assumes time-invariant pre-industrial land cover. This required a correction for sinks and sources on land subsequently converted to other uses. For GCB2026, three additional simulations (S4–S6) allow the land sink and its attribution to environmental drivers to be calculated using simulations with transient land cover. The land carbon sink is calculated as: SLAND = S3 − (S4 − S0) + δL where δL represents the transient environmental effects on land-use change emissions, estimated using bookkeeping models - and can be found at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23528902 The contributions from atmospheric CO₂ and nitrogen deposition and from climate are estimated as: CO₂ and nitrogen deposition: S3 − S6 + δL Climate: S3 − S5 + S0 These simulations provide a consistent framework for investigating terrestrial carbon fluxes under historical changes in environmental conditions and land use. Further methodological details are provided in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 Supplementary Information. Data availability Access and download the data: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ The complete gridded model output is hosted externally on Wasabi object storage and made available through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. The underlying NetCDF model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. This Zenodo record provides a persistent DOI, dataset documentation and information about the externally hosted release. Model contributions and coordination The TRENDY-GCB2026 simulations were contributed by international modelling groups. The creators listed in this record include the TRENDY coordinators and a representative of each contributing model. TRENDY coordination: Stephen Sitch, Pierre Friedlingstein and Mike O'Sullivan. Individual model representatives and their corresponding models are identified in the accompanying model contribution metadata. Release information This dataset corresponds to TRENDY version 15, the final version of the land model simulations used for the Global Carbon Budget 2026. Please use the naming convention "TRENDY-GCB2026" in publication/presentations. The Zenodo deposit contains the following files: trendy_listofvariables_GCP2026.xlsx — definitions and specifications of model output variables. TRENDY-GCB2026-manifest.csv — inventory of externally hosted gridded model output files, including filenames, paths, sizes and modification dates. TRENDY-GCB2026-model-credits.csv — contributing models, model representatives and TRENDY coordinators. TRENDY-GCB2026-data-policy.md — data usage, attribution and co-authorship requirements. The underlying gridded model output is hosted on Wasabi and is accessible through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser. These model output files are not deposited in Zenodo. How to cite this dataset When using the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output, users should cite all three of the following resources: Global Carbon Budget: Friedlingstein et al. (2026) — Global Carbon Budget 2026. This publication describes the Global Carbon Budget assessment, including the methodology used to estimate the terrestrial carbon sink. TRENDY model intercomparison: Sitch et al. (2024) — This publication describes the TRENDY model intercomparison framework and its application to understanding the terrestrial carbon cycle. [https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GB008102] TRENDY-GCB2026 dataset: O'Sullivan et al. (2026) — TRENDY Land Model Output for the Global Carbon Budget, version v15. Zenodo. [10.5281/zenodo.23561904]. This dataset record provides access to the gridded model output and formally credits the participating modelling groups. These three citations are complementary and should be included when publishing analyses based on the TRENDY-GCB2026 gridded model output. Users should also cite relevant individual model publications where appropriate. Citation of these resources does not replace the TRENDY data policy, including the requirements for prior circulation of manuscripts and invitations to co-authorship where the data make a significant contribution. Data use and licensing The underlying model output is provided through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser and remains subject to the TRENDY data policy, including its acknowledgement, attribution and co-authorship requirements. Users intending to use the model output in research or publications should consult the data policy and contact the TRENDY coordinators and relevant modelling groups as appropriate. The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence associated with this Zenodo record applies only to the documentation and metadata deposited on Zenodo. It does not apply to the underlying gridded model output hosted externally on Wasabi, for which the TRENDY data policy governs use and redistribution. The TRENDY data policy and model output can be accessed through the Global Carbon Budget Data Browser: https://mdosullivan.github.io/GCB/ Related publication Friedlingstein, P., et al. (2026). Global Carbon Budget 2026. Earth System Science Data, XX, XXXX–XXXX. [LINK] Global Carbon Budget 2026 synthesis data The official Global Carbon Budget 2026 data supplement, including the global carbon budget spreadsheet containing aggregated terrestrial carbon sink estimates derived from the DGVM ensemble, is available through the ICOS Carbon Portal: https://www.icos-cp.eu/impact/science/global-carbon-budget/2026 The ICOS data supplement and the TRENDY gridded model output are complementary resources. The former provides the published Global Carbon Budget synthesis results, while the latter provides access to the underlying spatially resolved terrestrial model simulations.

title: Land-Use Harmonization 2 for Global Carbon Budget 2025 (LUH2-GCB2025)
description: The Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUH2) dataset is updated every year for use in the annual Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations and publications. The LUH2-GCB2025 dataset represents the land-use data used by DGVMs and book-keeping models in the GCB 2025. It is extended to the current year using new input data from FAO and other sources, and extends historical trends for years without underlying input data. In particular, it incorporates new HYDE land-use data as a key input, continues to provide improved representation of deforestation in Brazil and Indonesia by using the latest versions of MapBiomas remote sensing data, and it improves cropland areas in China using data from Yu et al. 2022. For more information, see: Chini et al. 2021, "Land-use harmonization datasets for annual global carbon budgets", Earth System Science Data, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-13-4175-2021 Hurtt et al. 2020, "Harmonization of global land use change and management for the period 850–2100 (LUH2) for CMIP6", Geoscientific Model Development, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-13-5425-2020

title: LDEO-HPD: Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data pCO2 Product
description: Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data (LDEO-HPD) This collection contains the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory Hybrid Physics Data (LDEO-HPD) product. This product makes near-global monthly estimates of surface ocean pCO2 from January 1982 through December 2018 with a 1ºx1º spatial resolution. LDEO-HPD uses an eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) algorithm to make estimates of the misfit between observations and mode-based estimates. These spatiotemporal misfit estimates are then added back to the model-based estimate to make the final LDEO-HPD estimate. This is done for each of nine models part of the Global Carbon Budget 2020. Air-sea CO2 flux is calculated using a bulk parameterization, which is a function of wind speed. Three wind speed products are used to estimate flux. The average across these three estimates is taken as the best estimate. Datasets in this collection: LDEO-HPD_error_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of the misfit from each model LDEO-HPD_spco2_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of surface ocean pCO2 for each model LDEO-HPD_fgco2_v20210425_1x1_198201-201812.nc : contains estimates of air-sea CO2 flux for each model and wind product

title: ASSESSMENT OF THE IMPACT OF ENERGY EFFICIENCY IMPROVEMENTS IN THERMAL POWER PLANTS OF UZBEKISTAN ON ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND CO₂ EMISSIONS
description: This article analyzes the impact of improving energy efficiency in thermal power plants of Uzbekistan on electricity generation volume and carbon dioxide () emissions. The study investigates the technical and economic performance indicators of thermal power plants, which constitute the main generation capacity within the country’s power system. The relationship between thermal efficiency, fuel consumption, and electricity generation was evaluated using mathematical methods. The findings demonstrate that increasing energy efficiency reduces natural gas consumption and, consequently, decreases emissions. Furthermore, the effects of modern combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) units, high-efficiency turbines, and digital control technologies on energy efficiency were assessed. The results indicate that modernizing thermal power plants in Uzbekistan plays a crucial role in strengthening energy security, ensuring the rational use of fuel resources, and reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas emissions.

description: GCP-GridFED (version 2019.1) is a gridded fossil emissions dataset that is consistent with the national CO2 emissions reported by the Global Carbon Project (GCP). title: Land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) data for the Global Carbon Budget 2026
description: Description This dataset provides estimates of net land-use change CO2 emissions (ELUC) and their component fluxes from the three bookkeeping models used in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (GCB2026): BLUE (Hansis et al., 2015), LUCE (Qin et al., 2024), and OSCAR (Gasser et al., 2020). Peat drainage emissions are from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021), and peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). The dataset further includes the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026, including estimates from national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs) and atmospheric inversions. The dataset also includes global and gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL), which is the difference in ELUC between a simulation with transient carbon densities and a simulation with pre-industrial carbon densities. The reported net ELUC estimates already include the environmental contribution (δL). Net ELUC and its component fluxes are available as global and national annual time series for 1850–2025. Net ELUC is also available as gridded annual time series (0.25° resolution) for 1959–2025. The data describe CO2 emissions and removals expressed as mass of carbon (C). For ELUC and its component fluxes, positive values denote emissions and negative values denote removals. The sign convention for δL is explained below. Empty cells in .xlsx files denote missing values. The dataset contains 20 files: One .xlsx file with global estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) Fourteen .xlsx files with country-level estimates for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR, one for each of the net and component fluxes listed below (units: TgC/yr) Two NetCDF files with gridded net ELUC estimates for BLUE and LUCE (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) One .xlsx file with the data underlying Figure 8 of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One .xlsx file with the global estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr) One NetCDF file with the gridded estimates of the environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) (units: tC/ha/yr, referring to total grid-cell area) Global, country-level, and gridded data The dataset includes the following net and component fluxes. The identifiers shown in monospace are used in the corresponding country-level filenames and as worksheet names in the file with global estimates. “SC” denotes shifting cultivation, and “nonforest” refers to shrub and herbaceous vegetation: net-eluc (net ELUC): Net CO2 emissions from land-use change. clearing-allveg-total (deforestation and clearing of other vegetation (total)): Total CO2 emissions from deforestation and the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent clearing and clearing within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-allveg-total ((re-)growth of forest and other vegetation (total)): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of forests and shrub and herbaceous vegetation, including both permanent (re-)growth and (re-)growth within shifting cultivation cycles. wood-harvest-management (wood harvest & other management): CO2 emissions from the decay of harvested wood products and residues left on site, and CO2 removals through regrowth following harvest. cropland-pasture-urban (cropland-pasture-urban transitions): CO2 fluxes from transitions between cropland, pasture, and urban areas. peat-emissions (peat drainage & peat fires): CO2 emissions from peat drainage and anthropogenic peat fires. Peat drainage emissions are the average of estimates from FAO (Conchedda and Tubiello, 2020), LPX-Bern (Lienert and Joos, 2018; Müller and Joos, 2021), and ORCHIDEE-PEAT (Qiu et al., 2021). Peat fire emissions are from GFED5.1 (van der Werf et al., 2025). clearing-forest-permanent (permanent deforestation): CO2 emissions from permanent deforestation. clearing-forest-sc (deforestation in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from deforestation within shifting cultivation cycles. clearing-nonforest-permanent (permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 emissions from the permanent clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation. clearing-nonforest-sc (clearing of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 emissions from the clearing of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-forest-permanent (permanent forest (re-)growth due to re/afforestation): CO2 removals through forest growth and regrowth following permanent afforestation and reforestation. regrowth-forest-sc (forest (re-)growth in SC cycles): CO2 removals through forest regrowth within shifting cultivation cycles. regrowth-nonforest-permanent (permanent (re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation): CO2 removals through the growth and regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation following permanent land-use changes. regrowth-nonforest-sc ((re-)growth of shrub and herbaceous veg. in SC cycles): CO2 removals through the regrowth of shrub and herbaceous vegetation within shifting cultivation cycles. Components 2–6 sum to net ELUC (component 1). Components 7–10 are subdivisions of component 2 and sum to its total. Components 11–14 are subdivisions of component 3 and sum to its total. Environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) The environmental contribution to ELUC (δL) is defined as the difference in ELUC between simulations using transient and pre-industrial carbon densities (transient minus pre-industrial). Positive values indicate higher ELUC under transient carbon densities, and negative values indicate lower ELUC. Annual estimates are provided for BLUE, LUCE, and OSCAR in two files: GCB2026_Environmental-contribution-to-ELUC_global_1850-2025.xlsx: Global estimates for 1850–2025 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr). (2026)). Data underlying Figure 8 The file GCB2026_Figure8_Data.xlsx contains the datasets used in Figure 8 (a-c) of GCB2026 (units: PgC/yr = GtC/yr), within the period 1990–2025 for bookkeeping estimates and the sink in managed forests and for the period 2000–2025 for national greenhouse gas inventories (NGHGIs; 2024 data replicated in 2025) and atmospheric inversions. title: Data for O'Sullivan et al. (2025) "An improved approach to estimate the natural land carbon sink"
description: This dataset provides corrected estimates of the natural land carbon sink (SLAND) for the period 1959-2024, accounting for the bias introduced by fixed pre-industrial land cover in Global Carbon Budget (GCB) simulations. The correction is based on outputs from seven Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) participating in the GCB2025, using a novel method that combines PFT-level net biome production (NBP) from the S2 simulation with transient land cover from the S3 simulation. The dataset includes: Global fluxes: SLAND values for each model before and after correction. Regional fluxes: SLAND for 10 global regions based on the RECCAP2 regional definitions. Gridded fluxes: SLAND (0.5° x 0.5°) estimates for each model, including a version incorporating S3 land cover. The Replaced Sinks and Sources can be calulcated as the difference between the two SLAND estimates. This dataset supports the manuscript "An improved approach to estimate the natural land carbon sink". The corrected SLAND estimate brings bottom-up land sink values into closer agreement with top-down atmospheric constraints and alters the Global Carbon Budget imbalance, with implications for understanding carbon-climate feedbacks and climate policy. ## Note: The sum of gridded fluxes will not match the global/regional values exactly due to the regridding of DGVM output to a common 0.5° grid. Also, models require their own land/sea masks to scale gridbox carbon flux values - which is taken into account in the provided global/regional values.

title: Development drivers, CO2 emissions and ecological footprint in developing economies, 2000 to 2025: research database and R code
description: A documented panel of the 163 economies that the World Bank classified as low or middle income in at least one fiscal year from FY2001 to FY2025, with the R script that runs the whole analysis. The panel covers 2000 to 2025: 4,238 country-years and 119 columns. It is the research database of the doctoral dissertation "AI-Enhanced Modeling of Development–Environment Interactions in Developing Economies: Integrating Econometric and Explainable Machine Learning Approaches" (Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences, MATE, 2026) and of the journal manuscripts drawn from it. The panel holds two outcomes, CO2 emissions per capita and the ecological footprint of production per capita, and eight explanatory variables: population growth, GDP per capita growth, trade openness, urbanization, the renewable share of final energy, industry value added, energy intensity and mean years of schooling. It also holds alternative and extra series, sample flags and two break dummies. Every value of the ten core variables has a status (published, second source, estimate, nowcast or national source). 83 values come from national statistical sources under written rules, each with its publishing body, table and link. 46 gaps in the explanatory variables are filled by multiple imputation in 50 datasets. The R script reads the data file and produces every result table, from the checks of the database to the last robustness check: panel models, Random Forest, XGBoost, SHAP values and the checks on the 50 imputed datasets. A full run takes about 12 hours on a laptop. One series is left out of the data file. The 3,900 values of CO2 per capita that are computed from the IEA-EDGAR CO2 file of EDGAR 2026 are empty, because that file is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and its licence does not allow a database built from it to be shared. The file itself is included unchanged under its own licence, and the script computes the values again from it. The 250 values from the Global Carbon Budget are included, and so is the Global Carbon Budget series (column co2_pc_gcb). The column biomass_cooking (WHO Global Health Observatory) is empty because of the WHO terms of use. No result uses it. README.md says how to run the script. LICENSES.md gives the licence of each part and the terms and the citation of every source. Please also cite the sources of the series you use.

title: Advances and Integration of Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS): A Circular Approach Towards a Net-Zero Carbon Economy
description: Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels from human activities pose a major threat to global climate stability, reinforcing the need for effective mitigation technologies. Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) has become a central strategy for advancing a net-zero carbon economy by simultaneously reducing emissions and creating value from captured CO₂. Significant progress in carbon capture and storage has been achieved in energy-intensive and industrial sectors, with geological sequestration serving as the primary long-term storage option. Meanwhile, utilization pathways are gaining traction for converting CO₂ into fuels, chemicals, and construction materials, thereby promoting circular resource flows. Recent advances in CCUS are supported by innovative materials such as metalorganic frameworks (MOFs), solid sorbents, and amine-functionalized membranes, which offer improved selectivity, durability, and energy efficiency. Integrated approaches, including direct air capture (DAC), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), and electrochemical CO₂ conversion, further strengthen system performance and expand utilization potential. However, high energy demand, economic constraints, infrastructure requirements, regulatory uncertainties, and public acceptance continue to limit large-scale deployment. Addressing these challenges will require supportive policy frameworks and interdisciplinary research to enhance techno-economic feasibility and scalability. Most importantly, CCUS represents a critical pathway for achieving deep decarbonization within a circular and resilient global economy.

title: Role of the Amazon River Estuary in Land-to-Ocean Carbon and Nutrients Exchanges
description: Estuaries are biogeochemical hotspots that regulate the balance of carbon and nutrients delivered to the ocean. In the absence of land-to-ocean models, estuarine processes are overlooked in the global carbon budget. Here, we connected the watershed (Global NEWS 2), reactive transport estuary (C-GEM), and ocean-biogeochemical (ECCO-Darwin) models to quantify the estuarine contribution to carbon and nutrient exchanges across the Lower Amazon. The remineralization of organic carbon drives substantial CO2 outgassing (27 Tg C yr-1) along the estuary and reduces the organic carbon delivered to the ocean (-62%). However, the resulting increase in lateral fluxes of inorganic nutrients enhances primary production in the river plume region (+150%). The estuary enhances CO2 uptake in the river plume and the tropical Atlantic (+8 and +7.1 Tg C yr-1, respectively) and improves simulated air-sea CO2 fluxes in ECCO-Darwin. Our coupled model approach advances the implementation of models that reduces the uncertainty associated with land-to-ocean processes in the global carbon budget.

title: Gridded fossil CO2 emissions and related O2 combustion consistent with national inventories
description: Data Access Notice Please note that, at present, the data for a sample of years are provided in this data record due to Zenodo's 50GB data limit. Data for all years 1959-2024 can be accessed via the following link: https://opendap.uea.ac.uk/opendap/hyrax/greenocean/GridFED/GridFEDv2025.1/contents.html Product Description See Jones et al. (2021) for a detailed description of this dataset and the core methods used to produce it. Key details are provided below. GCP-GridFED (version 2025.1) is a gridded fossil emissions dataset that is consistent with the national CO2 emissions reported by the Global Carbon Project (GCP; https://www.globalcarbonproject.org/) in the annual editions of its Global Carbon Budget (Friedlingstein et al., 2025). GCP-GridFED provides monthly fossil CO2 emissions for the period 1959-2024 at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°. The gridded emissions estimates are provided separately for fossil CO2 emitted by the oxidation of oil, coal and natural gas, international bunkers, and the calcination of limestone during cement production. The dataset also includes the cement carbonation sink of CO2. Note that positive values in GridFED signify a surface-to-atmosphere CO2 flux (emissions). Negative values signify an atmosphere-to-surface flux and apply only to the cement carbonation sink. GCP-GridFED also includes gridded uncertainties in CO2 emission, incorporating differences in uncertainty across emissions sectors and countries, and gridded estimates of corresponding O2 uptake based on oxidative ratios for oil, coal and natural gas (see Jones et al., 2021). Core Methodology in Brief GCP-GridFED was produced by scaling monthly gridded emissions for the year 2010, from the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR v4.3.2; Janssens-Maenhout et al., 2019), to the national annual emissions estimates compiled as part of the 2025 global carbon budget (GCP-NAE) for the years 1959-2025 (Andrew and Peters, 2025). For full details of the core methodology, see Jones et al. (2021). Changes to the Seasonality of Emissions in GCP-GridFEDv2022.2 onwards The seasonality of emissions (monthly distribution of annual emissions) for the following countries/sources is now based on the seasonality observed in the Carbon Monitor dataset (Liu et al., 2020; Dou et al., 2022): Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, China, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, India, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom, United States. State or province-level data is used for Brazil, China, Russia, and the United States. This also applies for the Bunker Aviation and Bunker Shipping sectors. Seasonality is determined in the following ways for those countries/sources: The seasonality of emissions in 2019-2024 is taken from Carbon Monitor. The seasonality of emissions in all years prior to 2019 is assigned as the average of the seasonality from Carbon Monitor in all years excluding 2020 (due to the impact of COVID-19 on the seasonality of emissions in 2020). For all countries not listed above and all years 1959-2024, GCP-GridFED adopts the seasonality from EDGAR v4.3.2 (year 2010; Janssens-Maenhout et al., 2019) and applies a correction based on heating/cooling degree days to account for inter-annual climate variability which effects emissions in some sectors (see Jones et al., 2021). Other New Features of GCP-GridFEDv2025.1 There have been no changes to the functionality of the GridFED code in this update versus v2023.1.

title: Climate and soil mediate the effects of liana density on forest dynamics
description: Forest community dynamics is a topic of great interest in times when the global carbon budget is a widespread concern due to climate change. Among its effects, longer periods of drought and liana proliferation, coupled with land-use change, may endanger tropical forest carbon sinks. Here, in a 10.3 ha sampling of six Atlantic semideciduous forests, we investigated the effects of liana crown occupancy and large-stemmed lianas, as well as their interactions with climate and soil, on forest dynamics. We expected that harsh environmental conditions would enhance the negative effects of lianas on forest productivity. Our hypothesis was corroborated by the findings that the positive effect of lianas on tree mortality increases under drier conditions, as well as their negative effect on tree recruitment. In addition, liana crown occupancy was the best predictor of net above-ground woody biomass productivity, which decreases as liana crown occupancy increases. Our study provides additional evidence of indirect climate change impacts on the tropical forest carbon sink by increasing the negative effects of liana crown occupancy on tree biomass productivity.

title: Global 0.1° Monthly Anthropogenic CO₂ Emissions Dataset with Near-Real-Time Updates
description: This dataset provides global monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°, with the latest update extending through September 2026. The dataset is designed to provide a valuable resource for assessing the global carbon budget and the effectiveness of climate mitigation efforts. The estimates are generated using a deep learning–based framework that employs a convolutional neural network as its backbone and incorporates a mask fusion module to address spatially missing input data. The framework integrates satellite observations, meteorological reanalysis data, and temporal and spatial encoding features to estimate anthropogenic CO₂ emissions at a global scale. The data are provided in NetCDF format on a global 0.1° × 0.1° grid (1800 × 3600 cells) using the WGS84 geographic coordinate system. Each file contains monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates for all 12 months of a given year, expressed in tonnes month⁻¹ cell⁻¹. Files follow the naming convention ACO2_01deg_YYYY.nc, where YYYY denotes the corresponding year. The dataset is also updated regularly at doi: 10.12237/casearth.6a01788fe8a21d1686165027 A manuscript describing the methodology and dataset is in preparation.

title: Global, Regional, and National Fossil-Fuel CO2 Emissions: 1751-2017
description: This data product is a time series of Carbon Dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuel combustion and cement manufacture. Estimates of CO2 emissions are included for the globe and by nation back to 1751, and include emissions from solid fuel consumption, liquid fuel consumption, gas fuel consumption, cement production, and gas flaring. Per capita CO2 emissions and emissions from international trade (bunker fuels) are included as well; bunker fuels are not included in country totals, but are assigned to the country in which loading took place. Estimates are generated using the United Nations Energy Statistics database and the United States Geologic Survey’s cement statistics. Datasets produced from this group at Appalachian State University are located at https://data.ess-dive.lbl.gov/view/doi:10.15485/1712447, and are also located at https://energy.appstate.edu/research/work-areas/cdiac-appstate. Historic CDIAC data from Oak Ridge National Laboratory are located here: https://data.ess-dive.lbl.gov/view/doi:10.3334/CDIAC/00001_V2017. This dataset is the foundational dataset for the annual global carbon budget and other carbon cycle analyses that need relevant fossil fuel CO2 data. Within this data package are spreadsheets (.csv) of global and national estimates of CO2 emissions as well as text files of the ranking of each country’s total CO2 emissions and per capita for that year

title: JRC Global Proxy Maps of Managed and Unmanaged Forest
description: The dataset provides maps of Managed and Unmanaged Forests at a global scale, with spatial resolutions of 5 km and 50 km. These maps serve as a proxy for countries' managed and non-managed forest areas, produced to support comparability between independent estimates and national Greenhouse Gas (GHG) reporting under the UNFCCC. The methodology uses country maps of managed forests where available, but also makes assumptions where official data is not present, employing independent datasets that may not be fully consistent with national forest definitions when no other options are available. Here, we present the version 2.0 (2026) of the “Global JRC Proxy Maps of Managed and Non-Managed Forests,” which is used to “translate” DGVMs (Dynamic Global Vegetation Models) results into national inventory definitions in the Global Carbon Budget 2026 (Friedlingstein et al., 2026). Country-level results of this translation are available through the Global Land Use Carbon Fluxes Data Hub: https://forest-observatory.ec.europa.eu/carbon/fluxes. Compared to version v.1, in this version v.2 the managed forest definitions of several countries were updated according to the information provided within their Biennuial Transparency Reports (BTRs). This dataset will be updated as better information becomes available.
