title: Dataset and Analysis Code Supporting "Asymmetric Impacts of Supply- and Demand-Driven Flash Droughts on Leaf Senescence"
description: README This repository contains the processed datasets and R scripts supporting the manuscript entitled “Asymmetric impacts of supply- and demand-driven flash droughts on leaf senescence.” The study investigates the asymmetric effects of supply-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with precipitation deficits, and demand-driven flash droughts, mainly associated with enhanced atmospheric evaporative demand, on vegetation leaf senescence across the Northern Hemisphere during 2001–2024. The repository contains the processed datasets supporting the analyses and visualizations. Owing to repository file-size constraints, some processed datasets are provided as ZIP archives. Compression does not alter the data content, and the files should be extracted before use. Phenology_North_poly.csv contains annual satellite-derived vegetation phenological metrics for each grid cell across the Northern Hemisphere and was used for phenological quality control and anomaly calculation. all_GS_FD_years.csv contains the grid-year combinations with at least one FD overlapping the growing season and was used to identify non-FD years for calculating the phenological baseline. dEOS_poly.csv contains the resulting LSD anomalies derived from the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF). The term “EOS” used in the file name and scripts denotes the end-of-season phenological metric and corresponds to the leaf senescence date (LSD) used in the manuscript. phenology_poly_pentad.csv records the long-term mean timing of the start, peak, and end of the growing season, expressed as the corresponding 8-day periods for each grid cell. SMrz_drought_events.csv contains the flash drought events identified from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles using 01_FD_detection.R, including the original P1–P4 event timing indices, minimum soil-moisture percentile, onset rate, and cumulative severity. SMrz_drought_events_mean_environment_anomaly.csv contains flash drought events overlapping the growing season and their mean environmental anomalies calculated over the complete, untruncated P1–P4 event periods. These variables were used to characterize the hydroclimatic conditions of the events and as inputs for their subsequent classification into supply- and demand-driven flash droughts. final_FD_events.csv is the final analytical dataset and contains 1,141,551 event records. It retains the original, untruncated P1–P4 indices and was constructed by (1) retaining FD events that overlapped the growing season, (2) retaining phenological observations within the grid-specific median ± 2.5 median absolute deviations and grid cells with an interannual LSD standard deviation below 30 days, (3) retaining only grid-year combinations with a single FD overlapping the growing season, and (4) excluding non-target land-cover and biome classes, including croplands, and records with predictor values outside their respective 1st–99th percentile ranges. This dataset was used in the subsequent LSD-response, structural equation modeling, random forest, SHAP, and model-improvement analyses. Meanenv_EarlyGS_anomaly.csv and Meanenv_LateGS_anomaly.csv contain environmental anomalies during the early and late growing seasons, respectively, while Additional_data.csv provides the additional background and vegetation variables used to construct the predictor set for the RF, SHAP, and related analyses. The background spatial datasets include MODIS_IGBP0.1deg_type.csv, which contains MODIS International Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land-cover classifications at a spatial resolution of 0.1°; phe_poly_biome.csv, which contains biome classifications based on the World Wildlife Fund terrestrial ecoregions; and Background_MAP.csv and Background_MAT.csv, which contain mean annual precipitation and mean annual temperature, respectively. worldmap.zip contains the world map and national boundary files used for spatial visualization. The datasets supporting the response and modeling analyses include dEOSsig_supply_poly.csv and dEOSsig_demand_poly.csv, which contain the statistical significance of LSD responses to supply- and demand-driven flash droughts, respectively. RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_EVI.csv and RF_compare_supply_demand_matched_SIF.csv contain the random forest model outputs used to evaluate and compare the simulated LSD responses based on EVI and SIF. FD_ET_series.csv contains the time series of evapotranspiration anomalies before and after flash drought onset. The SHAP outputs from the random forest models are provided in shap_mat_EVI_demand.rds, shap_mat_SIF_demand.rds, shap_mat_EVI_supply.rds, and shap_mat_SIF_supply.rds. These files contain the SHAP values used to quantify and visualize the contributions of climatic, biological, and flash-drought-related variables to the modeled LSD responses under the two flash drought types. The accompanying R scripts perform the principal data processing, statistical analyses, and visualization procedures used in the study. 01_FD_detection.R identifies flash drought events from root-zone soil-moisture percentiles, calculates their characteristics, and applies the prescribed duration criterion of 4–12 consecutive 8-day periods. 02_phenology_extraction.R extracts vegetation phenological metrics from satellite-derived EVI and SIF time series. 03_FD_environment_anomaly.R retains FD events that overlap the growing season without modifying their original P1–P4 indices and calculates environmental anomalies over their complete event periods. 04_phenology_anomaly_nonFD_baseline.R calculates phenological anomalies relative to years without growing-season FDs and applies the grid-specific phenological quality-control and single-event grid-year criteria. 05_final_FD_event_filtering.R generates the final analytical dataset from the records processed in the preceding steps and applies the land-cover, biome, and predictor percentile filters. 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R conducts random forest modeling and SHAP analysis to identify the climatic and biotic controls of leaf senescence responses. 07_SEM_analysis.R performs structural equation modeling to examine the pathways through which the two flash drought types regulate leaf senescence. 08_phenology_response_significance.R evaluates the significance of phenological responses to flash droughts. 09_visualization_analysis.R generates the principal figures and statistical visualizations, and 10_visualization_SHAP_analysis.R produces the SHAP importance and dependence plots. The original satellite, reanalysis, and ancillary datasets are not redistributed in this repository, except for the processed background and boundary data used for visualization. The original root-zone soil-moisture percentile series and processed LAI time series are not redistributed because of their large file sizes; their data sources and processing procedures are documented in the manuscript and accompanying code. The original datasets are publicly available from their respective data providers, as documented in the associated manuscript. The deposited processed datasets and scripts provide the materials needed to evaluate the reported results and reproduce the principal analyses and visualizations. Code execution and software environment All scripts were developed and tested using R version 4.5.2 in RStudio under Windows. No GPU or other non-standard hardware is required for most analyses. Before running the scripts, users should replace the placeholder input, output, and figure paths at the beginning of each script with valid local paths. The scripts can then be executed directly in RStudio. The scripts are numbered according to their recommended execution order. Scripts 01_FD_detection.R–05_final_FD_event_filtering.R perform FD detection, phenological extraction, anomaly calculation, and construction of the final analytical dataset. Scripts 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R–08_phenology_response_significance.R perform the RF–SHAP, SEM, and significance analyses, respectively. The final visualization scripts generate the figures reported in the manuscript. The deposited processed datasets allow the principal statistical analyses and figures to be reproduced without rerunning the complete processing chain from the original satellite and reanalysis data. Using the prepared input datasets, all scripts except 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R typically complete within several minutes, although runtime depends on computer performance and data-transfer speed. The complete random forest and SHAP workflow in 06_RF_SHAP_analysis.R was run on a multicore server and required approximately four days. This script calculates one response–FD-type SHAP combination per run and should be executed for the four combinations of EVI/SIF and supply-/demand-driven FDs to regenerate all deposited SHAP objects. The principal R packages and tested versions were: data.table 1.17.8, dplyr 1.1.4, zoo 1.8-12, doSNOW 1.0.20, foreach 1.5.2, ranger 0.17.0, ggplot2 4.0.0, patchwork 1.3.2, RColorBrewer 1.1-3, usdm 2.1-7, ALEPlot 1.1, mlbench 2.1-6, fastshap 0.1.1, future 1.33.2, lavaan 0.6-17, raster 3.6-26, terra 1.7-78, sf 1.0-23, plyr 1.8.9, and scales 1.4.0. A complete README file and R session record will be included with the code archive in the next repository version.

title: Data and code for Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification
description: This archive contains the R code, dataset provenance, input-file fingerprints, summary data, validation outputs and reference figures supporting the study “Global vegetation trend decomposition depends on ecosystem type and CO2 specification”. The analysis covers 2000–2020 at a 0.05-degree working grid and distinguishes five temporally stable vegetation classes. Ecosystem-stratified generalised additive models include site random intercepts and AR(1) errors. The primary model includes a spherical spatial smooth and CO2; a matched 2 × 2 design tests sensitivity to these two terms. Trend inference uses Newey–West standard errors and global Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Global and ecosystem summaries use actual pixel area, with spatial-block bootstrap intervals and spatial-block cross-validation. The archive includes pooled out-of-fold level, trend and sign diagnostics, area-representative held-out trend shares, five CO2 spatial-support scenarios, and machine-readable CSV versions of all 30 parts of Supplementary Tables 1–9. The environment–CO2 baseline and unexplained-residual shares are descriptive co-directional trend components. Their association with composite human pressure is exploratory and does not identify causal effects of human activity. Raw third-party datasets, high-resolution derived rasters, site-level source and prediction tables, and model objects are excluded where redistribution rights are unclear. Users must acquire source data from the official providers and follow the documented reconstruction workflow. The included Natural Earth coastline is public domain.

title: Ensemble Dataset of Permafrost Thaw Conditions, Northern High Latitudes (>45°N)
description: Ensemble Dataset of Permafrost Conditions, Northern High Latitudes This ensemble dataset includes three raster layers that describe permafrost thaw conditions across the northern high latitudes (> 45°N). All raster layers are resampled to a 1,000 m pixel size in the North Pole Lambert Azimuthal Equal Area Projection (False Northing = 0.0°; False Easting = 0.0°; Central Meridian = 0.0°; Latitude of Origin = 90.0°), WGS84 Datum. Each raster layer is provided in GeoTIFF format. An ArcGIS Pro layer file (.lyrx) is included for each raster layer to maintain the color legend. The primary raster layer in this dataset is the Permafrost Thaw Index (PTI). This index measures permafrost thaw potential using a two-tier ranking system based on two variables: mean annual ground temperature (MAGT; Tier 1) and the trends of MAGT and active layer thickness (Tier 2). The PTI classifies permafrost into 10 ranks, with three ranks in each tier. Rank 11 represents the most stable permafrost, while Rank 33 indicates permafrost with the highest thaw potentials. Additionally, Rank 40 is defined to depict isolated patches located at the southernmost extent, which are immediately susceptible to thaw under current climate conditions. The PTI map is generated using an ensemble approach from a set of open-access satellite datasets. Three additional permafrost condition maps are derived by integrating multiple published products to address inter-product inconsistencies. 1 Permafrost PP Ensemble: This raster layer is a base layer of permafrost existence in percentage. It integrates three published permafrost map products, all of which estimate permafrost percent (PP): the Obu map (Obu et al., 2018); the NIEER map (Northwest Institute of Eco-Environment and Research, China) (Ran et al., 2022), and the annual European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative Permafrost_CCI map series (1997–2021) (Westermann et al., 2024). A mean filter is applied to the annual Permafrost_CCI series to produce a representative Permafrost_CCI. Areas with PP > 0% in at least two products are considered permafrost existence, and the ensemble PP is calculated as the median of these three products. 2 Permafrost MAGT Ensemble: This raster layer provides spatial distribution of MAGT. It also integrates the three aforementioned permafrost products. The Obu and NIEER maps estimate MAGT at the top of the permafrost table. The annual Permafrost_CCI series estimates ground surface temperature (GST) at multiple depths. In this study, the GST at 2 m depth is used as an MAGT proxy, and a representative Permafrost_CCI MAGT is extracted by averaging across the 25-year period. The ensemble MAGT is calculated as the median of these three products. 3 Permafrost Land Cover Ensemble: This raster layer represents land cover distribution in permafrost lands. It integrates three published global and regional land cover maps: (1) ESA LandCover_CCI (ESA LandCover_CCI Project Team and Defourny, 2019); (2) Global Land Cover Characteristics (GLCC) Global Ecosystems map (USGS EROS, 2018); and (3) Circumpolar Arctic Vegetation Map (CAVM) (Raynolds and Walker, 2022). In the ensemble process, a majority filter is applied to the annual LandCover_CCI maps (2018-2022) to extract the most frequently classified land cover type during this period. Following the GLCC classification scheme, classes are merged or re-coded, if necessary, to maintain consistency in ecological characteristics. In the High Arctic tundra, five tundra classes are specifically extracted from the CAVM map: barren tundra, herbaceous tundra, dwarf shrub tundra, low shrub tundra, and wetland tundra. title: Arctic glaciers mass balance from satellite gravimetry only
description: This document describes the LEGOS-Magellium mass balance dataset for Arctic glacier regions based on satellite gravimetry only. A similar dataset using an a priori based on DEM differencing has been submitted to GLAMBIE (Pfeffer et al., 2024). previously. The dataset submitted here does not use an a priori, but uses only satellite gravimetry data. The total mass balance is evaluated for five regions of the 6th version of the Randolph Glacier Inventory , namely the Arctic Canada North, Arctic Canada South, Iceland, Svalbard, and, Russian Arctic. The total mass balance of Arctic glaciers is evaluated mainly based on satellite gravimetry measurements. An ensemble approach updated from Blazquez et al. (2018) is adopted to evaluate uncertainties associated with the processing and post-processing of GRACE (Gravity Recovery And Climate Experiment) and GRACE-FO (GRACE-Follow On) data. The effect of land hydrology is estimated for each region, but not corrected in the total mass balance dataset, because of the small water mass balance values and large errors inherent to hydrological models. Total mass changes expressed in Gt are estimated from April 2002 to September 2022 for five RGI regions. The uncertainty on total mass changes is provided with a confidence interval of 95%. The dataset is provided in the GlaMBIE CSV file format. The data product has been developed in collaboration between LEGOS and Magellium within the scope of the hybridation challenge funded by the CNES (R&T Hybrid Spatial Gravimetry 2022/2023). Reference: Blazquez, A., Meyssignac, B., Lemoine, J., Berthier, E., Ribes, A., & Cazenave, A. (2018). title: An improved GRACE-derived groundwater storage anomaly (igGWSA) dataset over global land with consideration of most non-groundwater components
description: Accurate monitoring of global groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) is imperative for global water security and socio-economic sustainability. The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite has emerged as a prevailing methodology for estimating GWSA by deducting non-groundwater components from terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA). However, in most previous studies, the accuracy of GWSA estimation suffers from inadequate consideration of non-groundwater components. Here we present an improved GRACE-derived GWSA dataset spanning 2000–2019 at the global scale, namely igGWSA, by taking into account most non-groundwater components including glaciers, permafrost, snow, lakes, reservoirs, profile soil moisture, and plant canopy water. igGWSA demonstrated strong agreement with well-observed groundwater level and model-simulated GWSA in five globally recognized hotspots of groundwater depletion, with the absolute value of correlation coefficient ranging from 0.94 to 0.99. Compared to igGWSA, inadequate consideration of non-groundwater components poses a significant potential impact on the accuracy of GWSA estimation in glacier-covered regions, permafrost zones, giant lakes, and deep-soil areas. For example, neglecting glaciers and permafrost would erroneously interpret glacier melting and permafrost degradation as part of changes in groundwater storage, respectively. The igGWSA is expected to serve global water security research, especially under a changing environment.

title: Global maps of agricultural expansion potential at a 300 m resolution
description: Global maps of agricultural expansion potential at a 300 m resolution This repository contains data from “Global maps of agricultural expansion potential at a 300 m resolution” study. Abstract: The global expansion of agricultural land is a leading driver of climate change and biodiversity loss. However, the spatial resolution of current global land change models is relatively coarse, which limits environmental impact assessments. To address this issue, we developed global maps representing the potential for conversion into agricultural land at a resolution of 10 arc-seconds (approximately 300 m at the equator). We created the maps using Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models relating locations of recent past conversions (2007-2020) into one of three cropland categories (cropland only, mosaics with >50% crops, and mosaics with <50% crops) to various predictor variables reflecting topography, climate, soil and accessibility. Cross-validation of the models indicated good performance with Area Under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.88-0.93. Hindcasting of the models from 1992 to 2006 revealed a similar high performance (AUC of 0.83-0.91), indicating that our maps provide representative estimates of current agricultural conversion potential provided that the drivers underlying agricultural expansion patterns remain the same. Our maps can be used to downscale projections of global land change models to more fine-grained patterns of future agricultural expansion, which is an asset for global environmental assessments. Data description: We provide here raster maps of agricultural expansion potential for three categories of agriculture - (i) cropland only, (ii) mosaics with >50% crops, and (iii) mosaics with <50% crops. The source for delineating categories was the ESA CCI land cover data. ESA CCI land cover data recognizes additional categories of agricultural land, however some of them have limited spatial coverage. For that reason, we merged the rainfed cropland and irrigated cropland categories into a single category - cropland only, where a grid cell is largely dominated by crops. Rainfed croplands account for 87% of the this category, while irrigated croplands account for the remaining 13%. Mosaic categories were defined in the same way as in the ESA CCI land cover dataset. Numerical designations of these categories in the ESA CCI land cover dataset are 10, 20, 30, and 40 for rainfed, irrigated, mosaics with >50% crops, and mosaics with <50% crops, respectively. Global maps are provided at the spatial resolution of 10 arc-seconds (~300 meters at the equator). These files are available for three categories in the main folder with the filename prefix "Agri_potential_mosaic_*". The numerical value in the file name refers to the agricultural category type (10 - cropland only, 30 - mosaics with >50% crops, and 40 - mosaics with <50% crops). In addition to the 10 arc-second layers, we provide aggregated layers with the spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds, 5 and 10 arc-minutes, for coarse-grained applications and less computationally-intensive analyses. We provide the aggregated layer maps for the minimum, median, mean/average, and maximum values of the aggregated 10 arc-seconds values within the coarser cells. There are in total 9 files provided for each of the aggregated spatial resolutions. Repository content: Full resolution layers: - “Agri_potential_mosaic_10.tif” is the global raster map for cropland only category at the spatial resolution of 10 arc-seconds. - “Agri_potential_mosaic_30.tif” is the global raster map for mosaics with >50% crops category at the spatial resolution of 10 arc-seconds. - “Agri_potential_mosaic_40.tif” is the global raster map for mosaics with <50% crops category at the spatial resolution of 10 arc-seconds. - "readme.txt" is the text file with the basic description and the metadata for the repository. Aggregated layers: This folder contains files with a different spatial resolution (30s, 5m, 10m; see argument "RESL" below). File names for the aggregated maps contain the following information: “Agri_potential_aggregated_RESL_TYPE_CATG.tif” - "RESL" is the spatial resolution of the layer. Value is either "30s", "5m", or "10m", corresponding to spatial resolution of 30 arc-second, 5 arc-minutes, and 10 arc-minutes. - "TYPE" is the type of aggregated values. Value is either "min", "avg", "med", or "max", corresponding to the minimum, mean, median, and maximum values of the aggregated 10 arc-seconds values within the coarser cells. - "CATG" is the category of agricultural land. Value is either "10", "30", or "40", where category 10 is cropland only, category 30 is mosaics with >50% crops, and category 40 is mosaics with <50% crops. Raster metadata: Driver: GTiff Projection proj4string: +proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +no_defs Notes on use: Our conversion potential maps are useful for researchers and practitioners interested in downscaling projections of global land change models to a more fine-grained patterns of future agricultural expansion, or interested in assessing the locations and effects of future agricultural expansion, for example in integrated assessment modelling or biodiversity impact modelling. When coupling outputs with integrated assessment modelling, our maps need to be combined with estimates of the expected future demands for agricultural land per socio-economic region. In such a coupled approach, our global conversion potential maps can be used to spatially allocate the additional agricultural land demands. In this context, it is important to note that the modelled relationships between the agricultural conversions and our set of predictors may result in non-zero probabilities also in areas that are highly unlikely to be converted into agriculture, such as urban areas or strictly protected nature reserves. This implies that users of our maps may need to implement an additional map layer that masks areas unavailable for agricultural expansion. We also stress that our maps represent agricultural conversion potential conditional on the predictor variables that we included, implying that our maps do not capture the possible influences of other potentially relevant predictors. For example, our conversion potential models and maps do not account for permafrost, which may pose significant challenges to possible agricultural expansion to higher latitudes in response to climate change.

title: Data for: The start of frozen dates over northern permafrost regions with the changing climate
description: The soil freeze-thaw cycle in the permafrost regions has a significant impact on regional surface energy and water balance. Although increasing efforts have been made to understand the responses of spring thawing to climate change, the mechanisms controlling the global interannual variability of the start date of permafrost frozen (SOF) remain unclear. Using long-term SOF from the combinations of multiple satellite microwave sensors between 1979–2020, and analytical techniques, including partial correlation, ridge regression, path analysis, and machine learning, we explored the responses of SOF to multiple climate change factors, including warming (surface and air temperature), start date of permafrost thawing (SOT), soil properties (soil temperature and volume of water), and the snow depth water equivalent (SDWE). Overall, climate warming exhibited the maximum control on SOF, but SOT in spring was also an important driver of SOF variability; among the 65.9% significant SOT and SOF correlations, 79.3% were positive, indicating an overall earlier thawing would contribute to an earlier frozen in winter. The machine learning analysis also suggested that apart from warming, SOT ranked as the second most important determinant of SOF. Therefore, we identified the mechanism responsible for the SOT-SOF relationship using the SEM analysis, which revealed that soil temperature change exhibited the maximum effect on this relationship, irrespective of the permafrost type. Finally, we analyzed the temporal changes in these responses using the moving window approach and found an increased effect of soil warming on SOF. Therefore, these results provide important insights into understanding and predicting SOF variations with future climate change.

title: Geospatial Analysis of Road Conditions and Hazardous Factors in Communities on Continuous vs. Sporadic Permafrost in Greenland
description: Road conditions and hazardous factors were surveyed in two permafrost-affected communities of West Greenland, Ilulissat (underlain by continuous ice-rich permafrost) and Sisimiut (underlain by sporadic permafrost). Pavement damages, repairs, embankment structural elements, artificial drainage systems, water accumulations and preferential snow ploughing deposits were notably mapped and georeferenced in a geographic information system to form high-resolution spatial databases. In total, respectively 66 and 76 \% of the paved road networks of Ilulissat and Sisimiut were surveyed. Manual in-situ mapping took place in September 2020 and September 2021 in Ilulissat, while Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) equipment was used to map road conditions in Sisimiut in September 2020. The severity of the pavement damages was assessed according to the ASTM D 6433–07, Standard Practice for Roads and Parking Lots Pavement Condition Index Surveys, by ASTM International (2008). The drainage conditions were characterized following the recommendations in Cold Regions Pavement Engineering, by Doré, G. and Zubeck, H. K. (2009). This dataset comprises the geospatial layers of the road damage and hazard inventories created for the settlements of Ilulissat and Sisimiut. Each settlement’s inventory is provided in a ZIP-folder, containing the geospatial layers as geopackages and sorted following a thematic structure. Further information about each layer and its attributes can be found in the metadata PDF document.

description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Rasuwa region in Nepal and Tibet : https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/ We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades stereo acquired on the 16 October 2022, 4 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The collection includes two DEM: 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_20m_aligned.tif 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total DEMs in 2x2m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean’s dem_align implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). 2022-10-16_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the 2 m and 20 m described above DEMs retaining the highest resolution where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. The composites combine 109 EarthDEM strip DEMs, version 4.1 (Porter et al., 2024), from WorldView-1/2/3 and GeoEye-1 in-track stereo images acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. Each strip was co-registered by translation on stable ground, and the co-registered stack was tied to ICESat-2. Two sets are provided. The 2 m set is clipped to the affected corridor and has 1032 km2 of valid data. The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source, runout and upper corridor, with 1721 km2 of valid data. Both sets include median and weighted-mean DEMs, per-pixel strip count and normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD), hillshades, an ordered temporal layer set and a strip footprint index. The ordered layers are earliest- and latest-strip-on-top DEMs with source-strip and acquisition-date maps, their elevation difference and the apparent rate. No individual strip DEMs and no source imagery are distributed. All products are cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs in EPSG:32645 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 45N) with heights above the WGS 84 ellipsoid. NMAD layers are nodata where fewer than two strips overlap. 00_*.png files are quick-look figures. 1.1 Corridor 2 m composite (earthdem_corridor_2m.zip: earthdem_corridor_2m_<layer>_v1.0.tif) The 2 m set is clipped to the affected-corridor polygon plus a 500 m buffer, and the strips were clipped before compositing. The 88 contributing strips were acquired 2009-03-16 to 2024-01-05. The shifts exclude the common tie to ICESat-2 (dE +0.07 m, dN -2.44 m, dU -0.10 m) that was applied to every strip. earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_stats_v1.0.json: coverage and stable-ground statistics of dh_m and dhdt_myr. 00_earthdem_corridor_2m_ordered_qa_v1.0.png: quick-look figure of the ordered layers. 1.2 Source-rectangle 8 m composite (earthdem_source_8m.zip: earthdem_source_8m_<layer>_v1.0.tif) The 8 m set covers a 45.7 x 40.2 km rectangle around the source area, runout and upper corridor, and is not clipped to the corridor. The rectangle is the same as in the companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c). The 8 m composite combines 66 co-registered strips acquired 2012-01-15 to 2023-12-02. The median of date_median is about 2016.0, and the median of date_wmean is about 2016.5. The layers and sidecar files are the same as in the 2 m set (section 1.1). In this set the wmean has smoother relief across strip boundaries, and the median has a slightly lower NMAD against ICESat-2 (0.90 m vs 0.94 m). 1.3 Validation (validation_v1.0.zip) The validation zip holds the ICESat-2 comparison for each DEM: a summary table, and a figure and a statistics file per product (section 3). 2. Methods Each strip was co-registered by translation in three passes. The first pass used the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM (European Space Agency and Airbus, 2022), converted to ellipsoid heights, as the reference. The second and third passes used the median of the aligned stack. Each pass solved the horizontal offset with the method of Nuth and Kääb (2011) on exposed stable ground with slopes of 1-45 degrees. Stable ground is the ESA WorldCover 2021 bare, grass, shrub, moss and cropland classes, excluding Randolph Glacier Inventory (RGI) 6.0 glaciers with a 100 m buffer. Before each solve, differences more than 100 m from the median difference and outliers beyond 3 NMAD were removed. The vertical offset is the median residual on stable ground. A refit was accepted only where it reduced the residual aspect signature. The strips were composited with the NASA Ames Stereo Pipeline dem_mosaic tool (Beyer et al., 2018). SETSM (Noh and Howat, 2015) is the EarthDEM stereo software. The 2 m composites use only stereo-matched pixels. Pixels that SETSM interpolated were masked along with the strip bitmask, and they are about 2 % of the valid strip area. The 8 m composites apply the bitmask only. GLO-30 was used only as the first-pass registration reference. No GLO-30 values enter any product, and voids are left as nodata. Before compositing, obvious blunders of up to hundreds of meters were removed from the strips over the source area. The 2019 Pléiades DEM (Berthier, 2026) and other independent DEMs served as the reference there. Coordinates are ITRF2020 at epoch 2022.27, the median date of the ICESat-2 data. The composite surfaces mostly date from about 2016, and plate motion of about 4 cm/yr toward the northeast moves the area about 0.25 m between 2016 and 2022. The 2015-04-25 Gorkha earthquake displaced the area by about 1.5 m horizontally, partway through the strip archive. Each strip was co-registered separately, so strips from before and after the earthquake are aligned to the same stack median. 3. Accuracy The ICESat-2 reference elevations are 10 m segment fits to all ATL03 photons, limited to exposed stable terrain. Against these segments, the four DEMs have median differences of -0.02 to +0.02 m and NMAD of 0.81 to 0.94 m. The 2 m DEMs overlap 43,031 segments and the 8 m DEMs overlap 72,773. Per-product statistics and figures are in validation_v1.0.zip. The figures include a diagnostic Nuth and Kääb (2011) horizontal fit. 4. Known issues The DEMs have voids on snow, shadow and glacier surfaces. median and wmean combine strips acquired 2009-2024, so on glacier, snow and vegetated surfaces they do not represent a single date; date_median and date_wmean give the approximate date of each pixel. first and last take each pixel from a single strip, identified in index_first / index_last and dated in date_first / date_last. The first and last mosaics can have larger errors and more blunders than median and wmean. The latest strip is from 2024-01-05. Along the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi, differences against post-event DEMs include changes from the separate 2025-07-08 Lhende Khola flood as well as the 2026-08-26 event. Blunders were removed only over the source area, inside the 2019 Pléiades footprint (section 2). Elsewhere, isolated blunders can remain where few strips overlap. Check the count and nmad layers before interpreting a large elevation change. The companion HMA pre-event record (Shean and Bhushan, 2026c) is co-registered to the same frame; the 8 m medians of the two records agree on stable ground to 0.8 m NMAD. 5. title: Robust increase in observed heat storage by the global subsurface: Ground heat storage estimates
description: Dataset overview This dataset includes global estimates of ground heat storage (GHS) for the period 1960-2020. The time series were created by combining geothermal estimates from Cuesta-Valero et al. (2022) and values retrieved from satellite remote sensing products. The GHS data was developed and first analyzed in Cuesta-Valero et al. (2025). GHS values were obtained as the cumulative sum of estimates of ground heat flux, considering a typical value of thermal inertia for geothermal records, and an effective thermal inertia for satellite records. Geothermal and satellite data were reconciled considering a physical method and a statistical method, thus two global GHS averages are provided.These estimates should be considered as upper and lower boundary values for GHS. The mean GHS from the two methods is also provided and can be considered as the reference for the period of interest. Dataset contents The netcdf file contains the GHS estimates from geothermal and satellite data since 1960. The ghs_phys and ghs_stats variables include estimates for which the physical and statistical reconciliation methods were used, while the ghs_avg variable corresponds to the average of the estimates from both methods. The standard deviation values for each estimate correspond to the variables ghs_phys_std, ghs_stats_std, and ghs_avg_std. title: 13 October 2019 Pléiades (CNES) pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli catastrophic flood
description: Updated version of the 2 m merged Pléiades DEM where a ~10 m horizontal shift was corrected. =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal (Rasuwa) and Tibet : (see e.g. https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/2026/08/august-2026-nepal-tibet-floods/) We provide here pre-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from a Pléiades tri-stereo acquired on the 13 October 2019, 7 years before the event. Images were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES, the French Space Agency. The updated collection includes one DEM : 2019-10-13_PHR1A_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif =========================== Methods The three Pléiades images were processed by pairs using the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP, Shean et al., 2016, Beyer et al., 2018), yielding in total nine DEMs in 2x2m, 4x4m and 20x20 m ground sampling distances (GSD). The processing was done using as only input the stereo-images and their orientation information, as Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs). The parallel_stereo routine performs all the steps needed in the correlation of the stereo-images, yielding a pointcloud which is then gridded at three GSD using the routine point2dem. We used the semi global matching (SGM) algorithm and the set of processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). All individual DEMs have all been coregistered to the Copernicus 30 DEM using David Shean's demcoreg (https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/72886193) implementation of Nuth & Kaab (2011). Then, for each GSD (20m, 4m and 2m), the three DEMs are mosaicked using the median value. 2019-10-13_DEM_SGM_2m_merged.tif results from a merging of the three above DEMs retaining the highest resolution (2 m)where available and filling in the gaps with the coarser resolution ones. title: Shorelines, elevation transects and environmental data for Drew Point, Ak study area, 2019-2022
description: This record consists of the shorelines and their derived products, elevation transects and environmental data used for the Cryosphere preprint: Multiple modes of shoreline change along the Alaskan Beaufort Sea observed using ICESat-2 altimetry and satellite imagery. There are three primary datasets: ERA-5 contains hourly output ERA5 reanalysis dataset (Hersbach et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.adbb2d47) from a single pixel (-153.83, 70.87) from May 1st through November 30th for 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022. It also contians a list of derived open water days for each year. ICESat-2 contains the subsetted ATL03 photons (Neuman et. al, 2023, https://doi.org/10.5067/ATLAS/ATL03.006) for RGT 137 ground tracks 1r, 2r and 3r on 07 April 2019, 04 January 2020, 02 July 2021, and 31 December 2021, elevation profiles derived from SlideRule (Shean et al., 2023), and shoreline boundaries picked from the elevation profiles and Planet imagery. It also includes cross-shore transects used to project ICESat-2-derived changes into the local shoreline-perpindicular direction. Planet_shorelines contains shorelines drived from 3m multispectral imagery from Planet Labs (Planet Team, 2024) as well as their derivatiev products. This included shorelines used for year-to-year change (annual_coastlines) and for uncertainty analysis (uncertainty_coastlines). It also includes the derived year-to year-change (shoreline_change), the baseline and cross-shore transects used to derived these change estiamtes, and a table with our derived annual shoreline change estimates compared with previously published estimates in this region. More detailed information on each datasets can be found in each folder's README file.

title: Preliminary Canadian Landslide Database
description: This preliminary Canadian landslide database is a publicly available compilation of existing landslide inventories and original mapping. Version 14.0 of the database contains 31,005 entries of both landslide events (discrete recorded period of movement) and landslide features (slope with morphology consistent with past or ongoing movement). Landslide locations are provided as point features and include attributes for landslide type, material type (surficial, rock, ice, anthropogenic), point location type (headscarp, source, transport, deposit), qualitative location confidence (low, moderate, high), and an attribute for tracking the database version when an entry was last updated. Where available, additional attributes such as volume estimate, date of occurrence, trigger, contributing factors, interpreted historical interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR)-based displacement, and reference to previous work are also provided. Most landslides in the database have been identified using Google Earth and publicly available lidar. Online mapping applications such as HazMapper by Scheip and Wegman (2021) and Arctic Landscape EXplorer (ALEX) by Lübker et al. (2024) have also been used to identify landslides based on the changes in multi-spectral indices derived from satellite acquired datasets. As most of the landslides have been identified using remote sensing techniques (optical, multi-spectral, lidar, InSAR), landslide type attribution is considered preliminary, and no characterization of the current level of landslide activity or hazard are provided. The database spatial sampling biases includes detailed representation of areas with existing inventory and where lidar is available which allows for the identification of landslide features in forested terrain. Based on these limitations, the preliminary Canadian landslide database is appropriate for research projects and for use as part of the initial desktop review but must not solely be relied on for formal landslide hazard assessments. Version 14.0 includes the addition of 3,005 landslide features over version 13.0. Highlights of this version include the ongoing interpretation of InSAR-based deformation maps (NASA, 2025; NRCan 2025) to identify 726 slopes (up from 449 in version 13) with landslide morphology which were likely active with very slow displacement rates between 2016 and 2024. The recent availability of InSAR-based deformation information provides improved interpretation of slope processes that can be used to update landslide inventories and hazard characterizations. Nonetheless, InSAR techniques have limitations (e.g., Wu and Madson, 2024) and hazard characterization needs to consider the impact of radar wavelength, stack depth, processing algorithm, topography, vegetation, snow cover, satellite line-of-sight relative to slope movement, and rate of surface displacement. This means that large (> 100,000 m3), very slow (< 160 mm/year – Porter 2023), unvegetated, east-west moving landslide are preferentially captured in the InSAR data. As a result, the number of presently moving slopes in Canada with the potential to cause damage is significantly greater than captured in the database. The database entries with attributes recording interpreted historical InSAR-based deformation pattern are also derived from records that stopped in 2024 (NASA, 2025; NRCan 2025) or earlier (Choe et al. 2021). Their current state of activity/hazard needs to be confirmed based on site-specific investigations (field instrumentation and/or remote sensing). Another highlight includes the addition of a new attribute field to record the formation of a landslide dammed lake. Version 14 includes 789 present or breached landslide dammed lakes. Gullying, subsidence, and submarine landslides are compiled in a separate file as they are not typical subaerial landslide processes, but they can still represent a hazard to infrastructure. Point location and attribute data are provided as .csv file which can be imported in GIS software and as .kmz file for visualization using Google Earth. Summary statistics are provided in a separate spreadsheet. Summary statistics from previous versions are provided in the different spreadsheet tabs. Release notes from this and previous versions are compiled in an accompanying pdf document. References Choe, B.-H., Blais-Stevens, A., Samsonov, S., and Dudley, J., 2021. title: Data from: Spatial variation and linkages of soil and vegetation in the Siberian Arctic tundra – coupling field observations with remote sensing data
description: Arctic tundra ecosystems will play a key role in future climate change due to intensifying permafrost thawing, plant growth and ecosystem carbon exchange, but monitoring these changes may be challenging due to the heterogeneity of Arctic landscapes. We examined spatial variation and linkages of soil and plant attributes in a site of Siberian Arctic tundra in Tiksi, northeast Russia, and evaluated possibilities to capture this variation by remote sensing for the benefit of carbon exchange measurements and landscape extrapolation. We distinguished nine land cover types (LCTs) and to characterize them, sampled 92 study plots for plant and soil attributes in 2014. Moreover, to test if variation in plant and soil attributes can be detected using remote sensing, we produced a normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and topographical parameters for each study plot using three very high spatial resolution multispectral satellite images. We found that soils ranged from mineral soils in bare soil and lichen tundra LCTs to soils of high percentage of organic matter (OM) in graminoid tundra, bog, dry fen and wet fen. OM content of the top soil was on average 14 g dm−3 in bare soil and lichen tundra and 89 g dm−3 in other LCTs. Total moss biomass varied from 0 to 820 g m−2, total vascular shoot mass from 7 to 112 g m−2 and vascular leaf area index (LAI) from 0.04 to 0.95 among LCTs. In late summer, soil temperatures at 15 cm depth were on average 25 ◦C in bare soil and lichen tundra, and varied from 5 to 9 ◦C in other LCTs. On average, depth of the biologically active, unfrozen soil layer doubled from early July to mid-August. When contrasted across study plots, moss biomass was positively associated with soil OM % and OM content and negatively associated with soil temperature, explaining 14–34 % of variation. Vascular shoot mass and LAI were also positively associated with soil OM content, and LAI with active layer depth, but only explained 6–15 % of variation. NDVI captured variation in vascular LAI better than in moss biomass, but while this difference was significant with late season NDVI, it was minimal with early season NDVI. For this reason, soil attributes associated with moss mass were better captured by early season NDVI. Topographic attributes were related to LAI and many soil attributes, but not to moss biomass and could not increase the amount of spatial variation explained in plant and soil attributes above that achieved by NDVI. The LCT map we produced had low to moderate uncertainty in predictions for plant and soil properties except for moss biomass and bare soil and lichen tundra LCTs. Our results illustrate a typical tundra ecosystem with great fine-scale spatial variation in both plant and soil attributes. Mosses dominate plant biomass and control many soil attributes, including OM % and temperature, but variation in moss biomass is difficult to capture by remote sensing reflectance, topography or a LCT map. Despite the general accuracy of landscape level predictions in our LCT approach, this indicates challenges in the spatial extrapolation of some of those vegetation and soil attributes that are relevant for the regional ecosystem and global climate models.

title: Pre- and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and elevation differences for the rock-ice avalanche source area of the August 2026 Trishuli/Rasuwa catastrophic flood
description: =========================== Introduction On 26 August 2026, a catastrophic debris flow hit the Trishuli river in Nepal and Tibet. We provide here pre-event and post-event Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) of the rock-ice avalanche area from Pléiades, SPOT6 and SPOT5 stereo-images. Date were obtained thanks to the Pléiades World Heritage program of Dinamis (https://dinamis.data-terra.org/) and CNES. The collection includes three files: Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_pre-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_DEM_post-event.tif Rasuwa_mosaic_dh.tif =========================== Methods The post-event DEM is purely based on Pleiades stereo images. The pre-event DEM is based mostly Pléiades and SPOT6 stereopairs. A small fraction of the pre-event DEM was derived from 10 m SPOT5-HRS images. All DEMs were generated at a ground sampling distance of 4 m using the semiglobal matching algorithm of the Ames Stereo Pipeline (Beyer et al., 2018; Shean et al., 2016) and the processing parameters from Deschamps-Berger et al. (2020). A ground sampling distance of 10 m was used for SPOT5-HRS. All individual DEMs were first co-registered and vertically adjusted to the Copernicus 30 (GLO-30) DEM, masking out glaciers using the Randolph Glacier Inventory v7 (RGI 7.0 consortium, 2023). Next, the individual pre- and post-event DEMs were co-registered in pairs to construct the most accurate DoD possible. Finally, those individual DoDs were mosaicked in a single map of elevation difference. The uncertainty on the mean elevation change was calculated using the patch method (Dussaillant et al., 2018). This approach aims to empirically determine the uncertainty associated with the mean elevation change by sampling patches (or tiles) of stable terrain of various sizes to constrain the decay of error with increasing averaging area (Miles et al., 2018; Wagnon et al., 2021). The stable terrain was defined here as excluding glaciers and a buffer around the river channels where erosion or deposition has occurred. For a 1 km² averaging area, the 1-sigma (68th percentile) error and the 2-sigma (95th percentile) error were calculated to be ±0.8 and ±1.8 m, respectively. Beyer, R. title: glenglat: Global englacial temperature database
description: Open-access database of englacial temperature measurements compiled from data submissions and published literature. It is developed on GitHub and published to Zenodo. This version (1.0.0) of the dataset is described in the following publication: Mylène Jacquemart, Ethan Welty, Marcus Gastaldello, and Guillem Carcanade (2025). glenglat: A database of global englacial temperatures. Earth System Science Data 17(4): 1627–1666. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-17-1627-2025 Dataset structure The dataset adheres to the Frictionless Data Tabular Data Package specification. The metadata in datapackage.json describes, in detail, the contents of the tabular data files in the data folder: source.csv: Description of each data source (either a personal communication or the reference to a published study). borehole.csv: Description of each borehole (location, elevation, etc), linked to source.csv via source_id and less formally via source identifiers in notes. profile.csv: Description of each profile (date, etc), linked to borehole.csv via borehole_id and to source.csv via source_id and less formally via source identifiers in notes. measurement.csv: Description of each measurement (depth and temperature), linked to profile.csv via borehole_id and profile_id. For boreholes with many profiles (e.g. from automated loggers), pairs of profile.csv and measurement.csv are stored separately in subfolders of data named {source.id}-{glacier}, where glacier is a simplified and kebab-cased version of the glacier name (e.g. flowers2022-little-kluane). Supporting information The folder sources, available on GitHub but omitted from dataset releases on Zenodo, contains subfolders (with names matching column source.id) with files that document how and from where the data was extracted. Tables Jump to: source · borehole · profile · measurement source Sources of information considered in the compilation of this database. Column names and categorical values closely follow the Citation Style Language (CSL) 1.0.2 specification. Names of people in non-Latin scripts are followed by a latinization in square brackets (e.g. В. С. Загороднов [V. S. Zagorodnov]) and non-English titles are followed by a translation in square brackets. The family name of Latin-script names is wrapped in curly braces when it is not the last word of the name (e.g. Emmanuel {Le Meur}, e.g. {Duan} Keqin) or the name ends in two or more unabbreviated words (e.g. Jon Ove {Hagen}). title: Data accompanying "Summer drought weakens land surface cooling of tundra vegetation"
description: This dataset contains the spatial and meteorological data underlying the statistical analysis in: Rietze et al. (in press) - Summer drought weakens land surface cooling by tundra vegetation All code to preprocess, analyze and visualize this data can be found under https://github.com/nrietze/ArcticDroughtPaper. This dataset contains three major components: The drone-derived mosaics of multispectral, RGB, and thermal imagery. The training polygons used for the land cover classification. Meteorological and micrometeorological observations used in the analysis and descriptions of flight conditions. Internal data from the drone flights. Folder structure: └───data ├───landcover ├───mosaics ├───shapefiles └───tables ├───intermediate └───results Clone the Github repository before downloading this data and insert the contents of this dataset into the empty "data" folder from the Github repo. Cite as: Rietze, Nils, Assmann, Jakob J., Damm, Alexander, Naegeli, Kathrin, Karsanaev, Sergey V., Maximov, Trofim C.,Plekhanova, Elena, Schaepman-Strub, Gabriela. (in press). Summer drought weakens land surface cooling of tundra vegetation. Abstract (from manuscript): Siberia experienced a prolonged heat wave in the spring of 2020, resulting in extreme summer drought and major wildfires in the North Eastern Siberian lowland tundra. In the Arctic tundra, plants play a key role in regulating the summer land surface energy budget by contributing to land surface cooling through evapotranspiration. Yet we know little about how drought conditions impact plant-mediated land surface cooling by tundra plant communities, and related positive feedback to the high air temperatures. Here we used high-resolution land surface temperature and vegetation maps based on drone imagery to determine the impact of the extreme summer drought in 2020 on land surface cooling in the lowland tundra of North-Eastern Siberia. We found strong differences in land surface cooling among plant communities in the drought year 2020 and the reference year 2021. Further, we observed a decrease in the normalized land surface cooling between the two years using the water deficit index (WDI) across all plant communities during the drought year. This shift indicates an energy budget regime dominated by sensible heat fluxes, contributing to land surface warming. Overall, our findings suggest significant variation in land surface cooling among common Arctic plant communities in the North-Eastern Siberian lowland tundra and a pronounced effect of drought on all community types. Based on our results we suggest accounting for tundra plant communities if we want to accurately predict the impacts and consequences of droughts on land surface cooling and energy flux related processes such as permafrost thaw and wildfires. Acknowledgements (from manuscript): N.R. was supported through the TRISHNA Science and Electronics Contribution (T-SEC), an ESA PRODEX project (contract no. 4000133711). Drone data acquisition was supported by the University Research Priority Program on Global Change and Biodiversity of the University of Zurich and by the Swiss National Science Foundation (grant no. 178753). We would like to thank Geert Hensgens of VU Amsterdam for sharing the flux tower data at the research site with us.

title: Chamoli Disaster Pre-event 2-m DEM Composite: September 2015
description: These “fine-quality” 2-m DEM composites and auxiliary products were created using 38 cross-track stereo DEMs generated from 11 overlapping monoscopic Maxar/DigitalGlobe WorldView-1 and WorldView-2 images acquired between August 28, 2015 and October 5, 2015. The original Level-1B WorldView-1/2 (© 2015 Maxar/DigitalGlobe, Inc.) are available under the NGA NextView license. All unique stereo combinations between these input images were processed using the NASA Ames Stereo Pipeline v2.6.2_post (Beyer et. al, 2018; build d7eb7c8) and a modified version of the methodology presented in Shean et al. (2016; 2020). Input images were orthorectified at native GSD using the 30-m Copernicus DEM (converted to ellipsoidal heights) and cropped to the region of interest for the February 7, 2021 Chamoli event. Specific "fine quality" ASP correlator settings, beyond defaults (https://stereopipeline.readthedocs.io/en/latest/stereodefault.html): --stereo-algorithm 2 (More Global Matching (MGM)) --cost-mode 3 (census transform) --subpixel-mode 9 (SGM Poly4) --corr-kernel 7x7 px --subpixel-kernel 15x15 px Each output DEM (height above the WGS84 ellipsoid) was posted at 2.0 m with UTM 44N projection (EPSG:32644). Each output DEM was then co-registered to a filtered/masked version of the HMA 8-m DEM Mosaic v2 (http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4532391) using the demcoreg/dem_align.py utility (http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3243481). A final filter was applied to mask any DEM pixels with elevation values that differed by more than +/- 80 m from the HMA 8-m DEM Mosaic v2. Several DEM composites were produced from the co-registered, filtered DEMs using the ASP dem_mosaic utility (https://stereopipeline.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/dem_mosaic.html). The first composite is the per-pixel weighted mean of all valid elevation values (*wmean.tif). This approach uses a weighting scheme that favors spatially continuous coverage (as opposed to small clusters of valid pixel separated by nodata values), resulting in a more seamless, blended composite. The second composite is the per-pixel median of all valid elevation values (*med.tif). Additional composites were created for the per-pixel DEM count (*count.tif) and per-pixel normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD, *nmad.tif). The latter captures the spread of elevation values in the input DEMs and offers a metric of relative accuracy. Shaded relief maps (*hs.tif) are included for visualization of the two elevation composites. All files are tiled, LZW-compressed GeoTiff format with internal overviews (GDAL gauss resampling). Many of the input images include scattered clouds, often over mountain peaks (e.g., https://api.discover.digitalglobe.com/show?id=1020010042B88700), leading to nodata gaps and residual artifacts in the corresponding stereo DEMs. These problematic areas can be identified by their low per-pixel count and high per-pixel NMAD values, and we recommend that users mask or avoid analysis in these areas. Higher NMAD values are also observed over forests, steep slopes and open water. Note that the westernmost ~3 km of the composite is only covered by a single input stereo DEM, resulting in higher error and more artifacts. We chose not to crop this region, as it included additional portions of the affected river system. We hope to integrate additional monoscopic images over this area to improve future DEM composite quality. We performed a preliminary evaluation of the DEM composites for areas within ~1-2 km of the river systems affected by the February 7, 2021 event. We observed residual artifacts in places, and recommend that users exercise caution when performing quantitative analysis and detailed geomorphologic interpretation. If possible, the corresponding WorldView-1 and WorldView-2 orthoimages should be used during interpretation of the DEM products to distinguish artifacts from real features. title: Greenhouse gas concentrations in high-Arctic streams in northeast Greenland and their relationships with stream chemistry and catchment characteristics
description: Description: Dataset on greenhouse gas concentrations and driver variables in headwater streams in the Zackenberg area, Northeast Greenland measured during three field campaigns 2021-2023. Methods are described below. Field sampling methods The 18 study streams are located in the Northeast Greenland National Park, near the Zackenberg Research Station (74°28’N, 20°34’W). The area has a polar tundra climate with mean annual air temperature of -9.1 °C; July is the warmest month with a mean of 5.8 °C, and February the coldest month with a mean of -22.4 °C and continuous permafrost. Annual mean precipitation is 261 mm of which approximately 10% falls as rain (Hansen et al., 2008). The 18 catchments spanned a gradient from steep, sparsely vegetated slopes with shallow, coarse mineral soils and limited snow retention, to low-gradient, wetter catchments with peat accumulation and more continuous vegetation cover. At each site (50-70 m reach), we measured stream discharge using the salt tracer release method (Gordon et al. 2004), and specific conductivity with a Cond 3110 WTW portable meter. We measured stream width at 10 points, and water depth at 50 points along the reach. We filtered water samples in the field: for dissolved nutrient analyses, we used 0.2 µm membrane filters (Supor 200 PES, Pall Corporation, Port Washington, New York, US), and for DOC/TDN analyses we used 0.7 µm pre-combusted glass fibre filters (GFF, Whatman, UK). Samples for nutrients were kept frozen until analysis, while samples for total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) and DOC were acidified with HCl 10% to pH 2-3 and stored refrigerated at 5 °C. We also measured pH in the field. All water samples and measurements were made in the middle of the streams’ width and depth. We estimated dissolved CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations in stream water using the headspace equilibration technique (McAuliffe, 1971). In the field, we collected replicate (n=3) 50 mL water samples from the upper 10 cm of the water column using a 60 mL polypropylene syringe. We then introduced 10 mL of N2 gas into each syringe to create a headspace and shook each syringe vigorously for ∼60s. Finally, the 10 mL headspace was transferred into a 5.9 mL pre-evacuated borosilicate glass vial (Exetainer, Labco, High Wycombe, UK) until analysis. Sample analysis We analyzed nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) using standard methods on a Lachat QC-8500 Flow Injection Autoanalyzer (colorimetric analysis; Lachat Instruments, Loveland, Colorado, US; APHA, 2005), and quantification limit for NO3-N and NH4+-N were 4 and 10 µg N L-1, respectively. Samples for TDN and DOC were analyzed on a TOC-Vcph/TNM-1 analyzer (chemiluminescence analysis; Shimadzu) with QL of 0.055 mg N L-1. The QL for DOC was 0.02 mg C L-1. Dissolved organic N (DON) was calculated by subtracting DIN (NO3--N + NH4+-N) from TDN. All data below the QL were expressed as half of the QL (QL/2). In the laboratory, we measured CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations using a dual-inlet Agilent 7890 GC system interfaced with a CTC CombiPal autosampler (Agilent, Nærum, Denmark), configured and calibrated using standard gases as described in detail by Petersen et al. (2012). We converted headspace gas concentrations to dissolved aqueous concentrations according to Henry's law, using Henry's constant to correct for water temperature and atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979). For each gas and sampling event, we calculated the % saturation as %sat = 100 × Cw/Ceq, where Cw is the measured dissolved gas concentration and Ceq is the concentration in equilibrium with the atmosphere, calculated from Henry’s law as Ceq = KH(T) × pgas. Here, KH(T) is the solubility coefficient at the in-situ water temperature (Weiss 1974; Weiss and Price 1980; Wiesenburg and Guinasso 1979), and pgas is the atmospheric partial pressure of the gas, calculated from atmospheric mixing ratios of 415 ppm for CO2, 1.80 ppm for CH4, and 0.330 ppm for N2O and the atmospheric pressure at the time of sampling. Thus, water temperature was used both to calculate the dissolved gas concentrations and their equilibrium concentrations Catchment characteristics Terrestrial vegetation density across the study area was quantified using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) derived from Sentinel-2 imagery. Images were obtained from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub, selected for lack of cloud cover, with a spatial resolution of 12 m. The temporal window for NDVI data was specifically delineated to early July, August, and September 2021, and early August 2023, to coincide with the field measurements of GHGs. The data were corrected for atmospheric bottom effects, with acquisition dates stamped as follows: 9Jul2021, 1Aug2021, 4Sept2021, and 2Aug2023. All NDVI values were computed from the Red (B4) and Near-Infrared (B8) bands using the formula (NIR−R)/(NIR+R) within a raster calculator, subsequently producing GeoTIFFs of the NDVI. For each catchment area, NDVI distribution was examined, and the median NDVI was calculated using the zonal statistics tool in ArcGIS pro. In addition, for each stream catchment, snow cover was also derived from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. Scene classification maps were downloaded from the ESA Copernicus Open Access Hub for the same days and regions as the NDVI imagery. The classification map was then overlaid with the catchments using the zonal statistics tool to estimate the snow cover for each catchment. The scene classification maps have a spatial resolution of 20 m, i.e. coarser than the NDVI data, but fine enough to resolve snow patches within the study catchments (0.24–11.3 km2). Finally, the catchment area, mean elevation, and terrain slope were derived using ArcticDEM, a high-resolution global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for territories north of 60° latitude, sourced from the Polar Geospatial Centre at the University of Minnesota (USA). For this study, processed mosaics with a 2 m spatial resolution were used and subsequently down-sampled to a 7 m spatial resolution using average resampling to reduce imagenoise. Arctic DEM was employed in ArcGIS Pro with spatial analyst tools to precisely delineate and model characteristics of the small-scale headwater stream catchments. References Gordon, N. D., McMahon, T. title: A 1-km monthly surface air temperature dataset for Arctic land (2000–2025)
description: Monthly mean near-surface (2 m) air temperature at 1-km resolution over Arctic land for March 2000 to December 2025 (310 monthly fields), reconstructed by an ensemble of Random Forest, LightGBM and XGBoost regressors trained separately for each calendar month on station observations (CRUTEM5 station archive, release 5.1.0.0) with MODIS predictors: Terra and Aqua day-time and night-time land surface temperature (MOD11A2, MYD11A2), Terra and Aqua NDVI (MOD13A3, MYD13A3), MCD12Q1.061 LC_Type5 land-cover fractions, latitude and longitude. Elevation is deliberately not a predictor; the reasons, and the measured consequence, are given in the accompanying paper. What changed in version 3.0. The predictor values of the training table are now pooled from the same gridded stacks the prediction reads, rather than from a separate extraction of the granules, so that training and prediction use one source. The land surface temperatures entering training are screened with three checks of the GHCN-Daily quality-assurance system at their published thresholds (world-record exceedance, a climatological outlier check at six biweight standard deviations, and spatial corroboration against the nearest neighbours); 3860 values, 0.50 % of the land surface temperatures, were found to be invalid — seven satellite month-year composites had reached the table with MODIS fill values that had not been masked when the monthly means were formed — and are treated as missing. The gridded predictor stacks were checked for the same signature and carry none of it, so no field of version 2.0 was affected by that defect. The models were refitted and the whole record re-predicted. Hold-out accuracy at the 120 withheld stations improves from 1.50 to 1.48 °C root-mean-square error. Data are on the native MODIS 1-km sinusoidal grid (34 tiles h09–h26, v00–v02, mosaicked to 3600 × 21600 cells, pixel 926.625433 m) with 2-D latitude/longitude and a CF grid mapping, so no resampling has been applied to the values. Water pixels are removed with the MOD44W mask and Greenland is excluded. Each annual file (ArcticSAT1km_monthly_YYYY.nc, CF-1.8 netCDF4) contains: sat — monthly mean near-surface air temperature (°C), ensemble mean of the three models; sat_model_spread — the per-pixel standard deviation of the three individual model predictions for the same month, a measure of structural (model-choice) uncertainty. Both are stored as int16 with scale_factor 0.01 °C (precision 0.01 °C), zlib-compressed, chunked one MODIS tile per chunk. ArcticSAT1km_grid.nc holds the static 2-D lat, lon, the MOD44W land_mask and tile_index; ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc holds the monthly climatologies, the warm (April–October) and cold (November–March) seasonal means, the number of valid years per pixel and the mean inter-model spread. Note on coverage: a fixed subset of land cells never has a valid MODIS/Terra night-time LST retrieval. The pattern is static — identical in every month and year of a given tile — and varies strongly between tiles (measured examples, as a fraction of the tile's land cells: h22v02 0 %, h24v02 12.3 %, h19v02 43.4 %). There the missing night-LST predictor enters the models as zero, so the prediction rests on the remaining predictors and is less well constrained. Nothing is blanked and no quality-flag variable is provided; every file carries this note in its comment global attribute, and README_data.md lists it under "Known limitations". The climatologies in ArcticSAT1km_climatology.nc use the period 2001–2025 (25 years), the earliest period in which all twelve calendar months are complete, since January and February begin in 2001. MANIFEST_md5.txt allows md5sum -c verification, MANIFEST_sizes.tsv lists file sizes, PROVENANCE.json gives a machine-readable provenance record, and README_data.md documents every variable, the method and the known limitations. Processing code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23490034 (https://github.com/SeoyeonLee-rosee/arctic-1km-sat).

title: Global Monthly Mean Burned Area (km², 0.25°) Averaged Across 2019–2024 — Derived from ESA FireCCI Sentinel-3 SYN v1.1
description: This dataset provides global monthly mean burned area (in square kilometers) averaged across the years 2019 to 2024. It is derived from the European Space Agency (ESA) Fire Disturbance Climate Change Initiative (FireCCI) Sentinel-3 SYN Burned Area Grid Product, version 1.1. The FireCCI product (FireCCIS311) combines multispectral reflectance data from the Ocean and Land Color Instrument (OLCI) and Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) sensors onboard the Sentinel-3A and 3B satellites, complemented by VIIRS thermal anomaly detections, to identify and quantify burned areas globally. The FireCCIS311 grid product summarizes pixel-level burned area information into a regular global grid at 0.25 × 0.25 degree spatial resolution and monthly temporal resolution. For this derived dataset, all available monthly grids from 2019 to 2024 were processed to calculate the long-term mean burned area for each calendar month (January–December). The resulting layers represent the climatological mean monthly fire activity, smoothing inter-annual variability and highlighting consistent spatial and seasonal patterns in global fire occurrence and extent. Each GeoTIFF file corresponds to one calendar month and contains the mean burned area per 0.25° grid cell, expressed in km². The dataset is suitable for use in ecological and environmental analyses, including studies of fire-climate interactions, vegetation dynamics, biogeography, ecological niche modeling, and assessments of disturbance regimes. All rasters cover the global extent (-180° to 180°, -90° to 90°) at 0.25° (~25 km) resolution in the WGS 84 coordinate reference system (EPSG: 4326). Pixel values indicate the mean burned area (km²) per grid cell; zero values correspond to grid cells where no burned area was detected across the 2019–2024 period. File contents: FireCCI_BurnedArea_MonthlyMean_Global_0.25deg.zip └── 12 GeoTIFF files: FireCCI_BurnedArea_Mean_01.tif – FireCCI_BurnedArea_Mean_12.tif (one for each calendar month, January–December) Data source: ESA Fire Climate Change Initiative (FireCCI): Sentinel-3 SYN Burned Area Grid Product, version 1.1 Chuvieco E., Pettinari M.L., Lizundia-Loiola J., Khairoun A., Danne O., Boettcher M., Storm T. title: ESA Fire Climate Change Initiative (FireCCI): MODIS FireCCI Burned Area GRID product, version 5.1 (2023-2024)
description: This dataset includes only the monthly FireCCI51 burned area grids for 2023 and 2024. The files are derived from the MODIS FireCCI v5.1 product, developed within the ESA Fire Disturbance project of the Climate Change Initiative (CCI), but only the burned area variable aggregated onto a regular global 0.25-degree grid is provided here. Specifically, the dataset includes only the burned_area variable, expressed in m². No additional auxiliary variables from the original product are included, standard error, fraction of observed area, fraction of burnable area, or other ancillary layers. The files are organized by year and month for 2023 and 2024, and represent the monthly burned area in each cell of the global grid. These data were used as input to train the harmonisation model applied in the development of the MRBA60 product (Torres-Vázquez et al., 2026). The data are distributed in NetCDF (.nc) format, using a WGS84 geographic coordinate system and a spatial resolution of 0.25 degrees. The file structure preserves the essential metadata associated with the burned_area variable from the original FireCCI51 product. Previous years of the FireCCI51 product, covering the period 2001–2022, are the official release of the dataset and can be accessed through the original product record: Chuvieco, E.; Pettinari, M.L.; Lizundia-Loiola, J.; Storm, T.; Padilla Parellada, M. title: State of Wildfires 2025-26: Regional Summaries of Burned Area, Fire Emissions, and Individual Fire Characteristics for National, Administrative and Biogeographical Regions
description: This dataset supports the State of Wildfires 2025-26 report under review at Earth System Science Data (Burton et al., under review). It is an update of the State of Wildfires 2024-25 report (Kelley et al. 2025). The dataset provides annual data and final-year anomalies in burned area (BA), fire carbon (C) emissions, and fire properties (e.g. distributional statistics for fire count, size, rate of growth). Annual data relate to the global fire season defined as March-February (e.g., March 2024-February 2026), aligning with an annuall lull in the global fire calendar (see Kelley et al., 2025). The complete methodology is described by Burton et al. (under review). Citation Work utilising our regional summaries should cite both Burton et al. (under review) AND the primary reference for the variable(s) of interest as follows: Giglio et al. (2018) for MODIS MCD64A1 BA. van der Werf et al. (2017) for GFED4.1s fire C emissions. Kaiser er al. (2012) for GFAS fire C emissions. van der Werf et al. (2025) AND Kaiser er al. (2012) for the average of GFED5 and GFAS fire C emissions. Andela et al. (2019) for the Global Fire Atlas. Giglio et al. (2016) for the Fire Radiative Power (FRP) observations. Torres-Vázquez et al. (in revision) for the MRBA60 BA product. Giglio et al. (2024) for VIIRS VNP64A1 BA.
