title: Data from: "Cross-realm transferability of species distribution models – species characteristics and prevalence matter more than modelling methods applied"
description: Abstract This data contains occurrence observations (presence-absence) of 11 aquatic macrophytes from Bothnian Sea and Lake Puruvesi, and environmental covariates used to build species distribution models (SDMs) in paper "Cross-realm transferability of species distribution models – species characteristics and prevalence matter more than modelling methods applied" in Ecological Modelling. In addition to data files, also R code for fitting the SDMs is supplied, as is the R code to replicate the analysis conducted in the paper. The data is stored in rdata format (point data), without coordinate information due to data policy restrictions. The species in the data are Isoëtes lacustris, Isoëtes echinospora, Ranunculus reptans, Ranunculus schmalhausenii, Potamogeton berchtoldii, Potamogeton perfoliatus, Potamogeton gramineus, Myriophyllum alterniflorum, Equisetum fluviatile, Eleocharis acicularis and Elodea canadensis. The environmental covariates are bottom water salinity, turbidity, sandy substrate occurrence, colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM), surface fetch, sampling depth, total nitrogen and total phosphorus, and distance to closest Phragmites australis reed bed. Objective of the study The modelling objective of the paper was species distribution model (SDM) transferability assesment. Transferability was assessed using models built in marine areas in projecting the distributions of the target species in Lake Puruvesi, Saimaa, Eastern Finland. Macrophyte mapping data from Lake Puruvesi was used as independent test data, against which transferability of the models was assessed. Location The species data was collected from two geographic areas: Bothnian Bay (Baltic Sea) and Lake Puruvesi (Eastern Finland). The marine observations from Bothnian Bay were split into three overlapping areas (areas 1-3), to test the effect of input data gradient length to SDM transferability. The largest marine sampling area (Area 3) ranged from 62.95, 65.91 latitude and 19.14, 27.99 longitude. Area 2 ranged from 63.95, 65.91 latitude and 21.53, 27.99 longitude. Area 1 ranged from 64.91, 65.91 latitude and 23.82, 27.99 longitude. The Hummonselkä subbasin of Lake Puruvesi, where the macrophyte test data was collected, is located at 61.89, 62.05 latitude and 29.58, 29.78 longitude. Species data The species observations were collected using diving transects placed in the floor of the sea or lake, and species observations were recorded in 2 m22 grid cells separated by 10 meters along the transect or 1 meters depth, depending which criteria was met first. The species data was collected in 2010 - 2020 from marine area, and 2017 from Lake Puruvesi. All macrophytes in 2 x 1 m frames were identified to species level by the diver, and the data contained information on species presence or absence in each grid cell. The diving transects were conducted using systematic survey protocol used in the underwater inventories of the Finnish Underwater Biodiversity Survey Program (VELMU) (Frosblom & Virtanen et al. 2024). The locations of the diving transects were not randomly distributed, but were placed using expert judgement. As all our study species are macroscopic and relatively easily identifiable in the field (with the exception of possibility of mixing I. echinospora and I. lacustris), we consider the absences in our observation data to indicate true absences. That said, as the observation area is rather small (2 m2), it is possible that a species may be found in the site of investigation (e.g. a small lagoon) but be located outside the vegetation sampling grid. Environmental data Bottom water salinity The seasonal mean bottom water salinity was modeled using a generalized additive model with mean salinity as response, with log-link and gamma distribution for the errors. This was necessary to keep the resulting predictions positive. Bottom depth, CDOM, river influence and spatial location were used as predictors. Data from 448 locations were used and each location had a minimum of three observations. The model was validated using 30 % of the data left outside of the model fitting. The explained deviance of the model was 0.94 and the correlation between raw data and predicted values was 0.95 with few outliers. Turbidity Maps of turbidity (in FNU, Formazin Nephelometric Unit) were generated from Sentinel-2 Multi-Spectral Imager (MSI) observations using the Case-2 Regional Coast Colour (C2RCC) bio-optical inversion model, containing separate atmospheric correction and water quality parts. Before computing C2RCC, the original 10-meter input data was downsampled to 60 meters. The output variable of the C2RCC processor correlative to turbidity is the backscattering of total suspended sediments at 443 nm, which was further calibrated into turbidity (FNU) values using SYKE's empirical equations for coastal waters and clear lakes (for a similar approach, see Attila et al. (2013) and Sagerman, Hansen, and Wikström (2020)). Monthly observations of turbidity were aggregated into median composites to reduce the effects of cloud cover and other disturbances. Due to low solar elevation and ice cover in winter, the turbidity distribution maps are generated only for the summer months (May to September). The current processing covers years 2017 to 2021. An average raster layer was created from monthly observations as input for SDM building. Probability of sandy substrate Random forest model was used to classify sandy bottoms from Sentinel 2 MSI satellite images in shallow water areas. Identifying sandy substrate is based on the higher reflectance compared to other substrates. The model was trained and validated using diver recorded field observations in the Baltic area, and diver recorded and echo sounding observations in the freshwater area. For full coverage including areas beyond the shallow water, the satellite image classification was combined with boosted regression tree modelling result in the Baltic, and echo sounding based product in the freshwater region. The resulting layers were probabilities of sandy substrate with 10-meter cell resolution. CDOM We used different methods to estimate the CDOM levels in Bothnian Bay and Lake Puruvesi, based on biogeochemical model data and satellite images. For Lake Puruvesi, we applied the Finnish Environment Institute's (Syke) in-house CDOM algorithm to the Sentinel-2 MSI images processed by the C2RCC bio-optical processor (Brockmann et al. 2016). The observations in 10 m resolution were aggregated as monthly averages for each month of the summer season (May to October) from 2017 to 2021. For Bothnian Bay, we used Syke's in-house Sentinel-2 MSI CDOM layers (resolution: 60 m) aggregated as seasonal averages (1 Jul to 7 Sep). CDOM values are given as absorption coefficient of CDOM at 400 nm [m⁻¹]. Surface fetch A surface fetch raster was produced to the Puruvesi and Bothnian Bay. The analysis required a feature layer of shorelines from Puruvesi and Baltic Sea. First, we created polyline from north to south spanning over the whole area of interest with a gap of 20 meters which is also the resolution of the output raster. These lines were then cut each time they hit the shoreline and the part of the line that was overlapping land was removed. The distance of the remaining lines was then calculated and a point with the distance value was created every 20 meters. Each time the line was cut when hitting an island for example and starting again from the other side of the island, the distance calculation started from 0. This created a point dataset with a distance value in each point. We repeated the procedure for 15 times for different compass directions with 22.5 degree intervals and calculated average fetch for each point location on 20 meters grid from these 15 point layers. Depth Depth was measured by a diver using a dive computer while surveying each vegetation grid cell, and measured depth was used when projecting model results to Puruvesi (transferability performance). In addition, a depth model for the freshwater region was created from Sentinel 2 MSI satellite image using the logarithmic band ratio model of blue and red band. The model was calibrated using diver recorded field observations and validated against echo sounding measurements. For more complete coverage and to include deep areas, echo soundings from multiple sources were combined with the satellite derived bathymetry. The cell resolution of the resulting depth layer was 10 meters. Total nitrogen and phosphorus Mean total nitrogen and phosphorus layers for marine area were produced using ArcGIS "splines with barriers" tool for the EEZ of Finland with 20 meters spatial resolution (Virtanen et al. 2018). Summer (July - September) nutrient measurements from 0 to 10 meters depth between 2010 and 2020, obtained from the VESLA database, were used as input data for the interpolation. Nitrogen and phosphorus measurements in Puruvesi between 2010 and 2020 was gathered from the VESLA database. Data from July to September was selected to represent the growing season. A mean value of NTOT and PTOT was then calculated for each location. Spline with Barriers (SwB) tool was used to interpolate the values (Arcmap 10.7.1). The tool uses a feature layer as barrier to create the raster representing only the area of interest. For the barrier and the extent of the interpolated raster we used a shapefile representing Lake Puruvesi shoreline. The resolution was set to 5x5 meters. SwB tool created an "extent box" around the area of interest which was removed with Extract by Mask tool using the shoreline feature layer. After the interpolation we noticed that either one of the locations was situated on land or the polygon used as barrier was "leaking". SwB doesn´t interpolate areas that doesn't have locations with values or aren´t connected to the main body of water. To fix this, the raster was extended outwards based on the values of nearby cells and after that the raster was masked again to remove any cells on land. The phosphorus interpolation provided negative values in southern parts on Enanlahti in Kontiolahti and Muholanlahti. These negative values were caused by considerably larger phosphorus values in Enanlahti Lamminniemi (9m) Enanlahti Lamminniemi (4m) locations when compared with the nearby Puruvesi Enanlahti location. The interpolation apparently continued to decrease the values according to the trend set by the difference between these locations and caused it to reach negative values. The southern parts of the bay, about 750 meters, was removed and new values were calculated based on the surrounding cells with Focal Statistics tool. The interpolations were validated by removing 20 % of the locations and reproducing the interpolation. The removed locations and their values were then compared to the interpolated raster. R∗2∗2 value from phosphorus interpolation model was 0.91 after removing two outliers and R22 value from nitrogen interpolation model was 0.715 after removing one outlier. Distance to closest reed The aquatic vegetation (Phragmites australis reeds) presence/absence maps were also generated from Sentinel-2 MSI data. The processing included extracting one month of data (July 2019) from green and near-infra-red bands from Sentinel-2 Global Mosaic (S2GM) service and transforming those to normalized-difference vegetation indices (NDVIs). After that, Bayesian statistics were used to predict the posterior probability of vegetation occurrence when distance from shore and NDVI were used as predictor variables. The posterior variable was thresholded and the resulting vegetation presence areas were sieved so that both too small vegetation areas (fewer than 5 pixels) or areas that were not directly attached to shoreline were removed. The resulting map has 10 m pixel size and tentatively represents the locations of reed belts or other shoreline-attached vegetation. This EO-based layer could also be referred to as helophytes or helophytic macrophytes, as it denotes a specific zone of vegetation with emergent aquatic plants containing leaf-green, particularly those that grow densely and have horizontally oriented leaves. In some lakes, this layer can represent, for example, thick stands of Equisetum fluviatile, although in most cases, it is associated with common reed belts. The approach is described in more detail in Koponen et al. (2022). Data partitioning Data was partitioned with 70/30 splitting into training and test (interpolation accuracy) data. The splitting was repeated 100 times for each species by randomly selecting 70 % of observations which were used to build each of the SDMs (GLM, GAM, BRT and BART). The partitioning was repeated for each of the three input data areas and 11 species. The input data indexes for replicating the split are supplied in the data files. R code Code files contain scripts for fitting the SDM models described in the paper using the data. Also code for calculating calidation statistics (modelling results) and code for statistical analyses for making inferences in the paper, are supplied. Additional info More details on modelling protocol may be found in the original paper in Ecological Modelling, and in the Supplementary Information file of the original paper, which follows the model reporting template "ODMAP" by Zurell et al. (2022). The LUTs and parameterizations were subsequently updated, and the current implementation is described in the S5P-PAL Product User Manual (PUM) (S5P-PAL data portal). For the ESA 4DMedSea project, these products were aggregated into temporal and spatial scales suitable for clustering the Mediterranean Sea into ecological regions. Validation was performed against BGC-Argo profiles and additional in-situ datasets. Data files are provided in NetCDF format, bundled into two compressed archives (PFT.zip and KD.zip). Each archive contains monthly fields for the full time period. These datasets support studies of phytoplankton diversity, dissolved organic matter (DOM), and underwater light availability in the surface ocean, particularly in the Mediterranean Sea.

title: ISOP synthetic ocean temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific, 2015
description: Daily ISOP (Improved Synthetic Ocean Profile) synthetic temperature and salinity profiles for the Northwestern Pacific (99°E–170°E, 20°S–66°N) for 1 January–31 December 2015. The product was developed by the authors following the methodology of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (Helber et al., 2013), with minor modifications. As described in the accompanying manuscript (Dan et al.), ISOP employs a three-layer vertical structure model (mixed layer, thermocline layer and deep quiescent layer) and uses a variational method combined with historical profile EOF statistics to project satellite sea surface observations onto the subsurface, generating three-dimensional temperature and salinity fields. Its satellite inputs are OISSTv2.1 daily 1/4° sea surface temperature, AVISO/DUACS global 1/8° multi-satellite merged sea surface height anomaly, and the Copernicus 1/8° sea surface salinity merged product. The product extends to a maximum depth of 1000 m (47 levels) at 1/4° horizontal resolution. Observational validation shows that its temperature and salinity errors are comparable to those of the HYCOM and GLORYS12V1 reanalyses, with grid-point temporal and daily spatial correlation coefficients of steric sea surface height with AVISO SLA of 0.874 and 0.897, respectively. The archive contains 365 daily NetCDF files named YYYYMMDD_isop.nc (20150101–20151231); temperature is in degrees Celsius and salinity in PSU, with missing values masked. Data are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Contact: Bo Dan (danb1991@163.com).

title: Global Daily Satellite-Derived Lake Surface Water Quality Dataset (2002-2022)
description: This repository hosts a standardized, accessible dataset of concurrent daily water quality statistics for 5,551 lakes worldwide from 2002 to 2022. Derived from the European Space Agency's Lakes Climate Change Initiative (ESA Lakes_cci) v2.1 and intersected with HydroLAKES v1.0 polygon boundaries, the dataset provides lake-wide statistics (minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, valid pixel count, spatial coverage ratio) for three water quality parameters: chlorophyll-a (Chl-a, mg m⁻³), lake surface water temperature (LSWT, °C), and turbidity (NTU). Records are temporally harmonized to retain only days on which all three parameters are simultaneously valid. A multi-tiered QA/QC flagging scheme is included to identify spatial inhomogeneities and temporal anomalies. Repository contents: hylak_id_description.csv — 47-column summary metadata file (central coordinates, country, Köppen-Geiger climate zone, valid observation counts, and long-term monthly/year-round means) for all 5,551 lakes. hylak_id.zip — 5,551 individual CSV files (one per lake, named {hylak_id}.csv), each containing the 22-column daily time series with QA/QC flags. code.zip — Python (v3.10) scripts used for data extraction, spatial masking, zonal statistics, harmonization, and QA/QC flagging. Full methodology, variable definitions, and validation are described in the companion paper (DOI to be added after publication).

title: ASSESSING THE CHLOROPHYLL-A VARIABILITY IN THE GULF OF GUINEA USING REMOTE SENSING DATA.
description: Introduction The report begins by highlighting the importance of oceans in influencing the Earth’s climate and supporting marine life. It focuses on phytoplankton, which are crucial for the marine food web and global carbon cycle. The study aims to evaluate the variability of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and sea surface temperature (SST) in the Gulf of Guinea using satellite remote sensing data. Materials and Methods Study Site: The Gulf of Guinea, located on the eastern edge of the Atlantic Ocean, bordered by several West African countries. Data: Monthly Chl-a and SST data from the Aqua-MODIS satellite, covering the period from 2020 to 2022. Methods: Analysis of satellite images using Python programming to evaluate spatiotemporal variability and conduct time series analysis. Results and Discussion Chlorophyll-a Variability: The study found significant spatial and temporal variability in Chl-a concentrations, with higher values near the coastline due to nutrient inputs from rivers and coastal upwelling. Sea Surface Temperature Variability: SST showed relatively uniform spatial distribution but notable seasonal and interannual variability, influenced by climatic phenomena like the West African Monsoon. Interannual and Monthly Climatology Variability: The report discusses the seasonal patterns and the influence of environmental factors on Chl-a and SST. Conclusion The study concludes that Chl-a concentrations are higher near the coast due to nutrient inputs and coastal upwelling, while SST shows a consistent seasonal cycle. These findings provide insights into the dynamic nature of marine productivity in the Gulf of Guinea and the influence of environmental factors on phytoplankton biomass.

title: Statistical blending of global-gridded climatological products: an approach to inverse hydrological model
description: The growing use of global-scale environmental products in hydro-climatic modeling (with different assumptions, resolutions, and precisions) has increased the variety of their applications and the complications of their uncertainties and evaluations. Researchers have recently turned to statistical blending (fusion) of these products to achieve optimal modeling while avoiding difficulties. The proposed statistical blending in this study includes five large-scale and satellite precipitation (Climate Hazards Group Infrared Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS), ERA5-Land of ECMWF (ERA), Integrated Multi-Satellite Retrievals for GPM (IMERG), Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM), and Terra) and evapotranspiration (Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM), SSEBop, Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Terra, and ERA) products committed in three modeling scenarios. The blending procedures are organized using a conceptual water balance model to achieve the best precipitation and evapotranspiration results for the conceptual production of streamflow using hydrological inverse modeling. Based on the results, the proposed blending procedures of precipitation and evapotranspiration improved the performance of the model using different statistical metrics. In addition, the results show the conformity of the pattern and behavior of the blended precipitation calculated using the moving least square method in the study area. This happened by changing the estimation based on in situ values, particularly in cold months considering the orographic/snow effects. The combining method provides a good fusion procedure to improve the realistic estimation of precipitation and evapotranspiration in ungagged watersheds as well.

Four ETo sources compared against the reference: Reference (ground truth): Xavier et al. BR-DWGD (0.1° ≈ 10 km resolution). NASA POWER ETo, computed in-house with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith engine (underlying reanalysis: MERRA-2, ~0.5° × 0.625°). Open-Meteo ETo, computed in-house with FAO-56 PM (underlying reanalysis: ERA5-Land, ~9 km). Open-Meteo API ETo, pre-computed by the Open-Meteo service (ERA5-Land), used as an independent benchmark. EVAonline — Adaptive Kalman Fusion product ⭐. 📂 Repository Structure 📁 data/ — raw inputs, intermediate files, descriptive statistics, per-source ETo, per-city validations, the four-source comparison, sensitivity analyses, and final figures. 📁 notebooks/ — demonstration notebooks for each provider (NASA POWER, Open-Meteo Archive/Forecast, MET Norway, NWS Forecast, NWS Stations) plus utility examples. 📁 scripts/ — API adapters (NASA POWER, Open-Meteo, MET Norway, NWS, OpenTopoData), the Kalman fusion core, the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith engine, and the sequential pipeline (scripts 1–7) to reproduce every manuscript result, including the two sensitivity scripts. 📁 validation/ — supplementary, unit-tested validation analyses reported in the article: temporal-split + leave-one-site-out cross-validation, site-wise metrics (median/IQR/min–max across the 17 sites), a component ablation (variable/component importance), and the error-boxplot figure. title: Data and code for comparing the cooling of urban water bodies and green spaces across the aridity gradient of 229 Chinese cities
description: This record contains the data and the code of the main calculations of a study that compares the daytime and nighttime land surface temperature (LST) of urban water bodies, green spaces and built-up land in 229 Chinese cities on a 1 km grid (June–August, 2018–2023). Contents: data/cells_1km.csv.gz: 746,554 cells of 1 km with LST by day and night, water occurrence, vegetation and built-up shares, elevation, background air and dewpoint temperature, NDVI, evapotranspiration and residents; data/cities.csv: the 229 cities with their aridity index and zone and summer climate; data/results/: city-level and station-level results underlying the figures and tables of the paper; code/: Python code of the main calculations (cooling intensity, the adjusted advantage of Eq. 1, the cover effects of Eq. 2 and the water demand), with a README that lists the variables, sources and steps. Source datasets: Global Urban Boundaries, MODIS Aqua LST (MYD11A2, MYD11A1), ESA WorldCover v200, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land, TerraClimate, MODIS NDVI (MOD13A2), ET (MOD16A2GF) and albedo (MCD43A3), PML-V2.2a, Landsat 8 and 9 Collection 2, WorldPop 2020, gridded GDP per capita (Kummu et al., 2025) and the Integrated Surface Database. Only derived values are included; the source data are available from their providers. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information 2026.

title: MOD-LSP: MODIS-Based Parameters for Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) Model over the Continental US, Mexico, and Southern Canada
description: The MOD-LSP project contains MODIS-based land and surface (soil and vegetation) parameters for the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model (Liang et al., 1994), release 5.0 and later (Hamman et al., 2018). The MOD-LSP spatial domain covers the continental United States, Mexico, and southern Canada; the associated domain files can be found in the PITRI archive (Bohn et al. 2018). This spatial domain and 0.625° (6 km) grid resolution are compatible with the gridded daily meteorological forcings of Livneh et al. (2015) ("L2015" hereafter) (http://ciresgroups.colorado.edu/livneh/data/daily-observational-hydrometeorology-data-set-north-american-extent), which can be disaggregated to hourly time step via the MetSim tool (Bennett et al. 2018) using the aforementioned PITRI domain files (Bohn et al. 2018). These parameters have two main purposes: (1) to improve upon previous widely-used parameters over the region (e.g., L2015) with updated, higher-resolution land cover maps and spatially explicit observations of surface properties; and (2) to expand from a single parameter set corresponding to one point in time to a series of parameter sets that account for temporal variability at seasonal to decadal scales. A detailed description of methods, the data sources and purposes of different VIC parameter sets within MOD-LSP, and how to use them with VIC, can be found in the MOD-LSP User Guide.pdf, included here. The scripts that were used to create the MOD-LSP parameters are archived on Zenodo and GitHub (Bohn 2019). If you wish to present or publish results that use these parameter sets, please cite the following paper: Bohn, T. J., and E. R. Vivoni, 2019b: MOD-LSP, MODIS-based land surface properties for assessing land cover variability and change over North America. Sci. Data, 6, 144, doi: 10.1038/s41597-019-0150-2. In addition, if you use the domain files associated with the PITRI precipitation disaggregation to accompany the MOD-LSP parameter files in VIC simulations, please cite the following paper: Bohn, T. J., K. M. Whitney, G. Mascaro, and E. R. Vivoni, 2019: A deterministic approach for approximating the diurnal cycle of precipitation for use in large-scale hydrological modeling. J. Hydrometeorol., 20, 297–317, doi:10.1175/JHM-D-18-0203.1. Contents: MOD-LSP User Guide v1.0.pdf - Explains how parameters were generated and how to set up the files for input in VIC simulations. global_param.template - Template for global_parameter file, which lists the locations of the other input files and sets various simulation options. The template contains placeholders for some filenames and simulation options, which must be replaced with real values by the user. params.$DOMAIN.L2015.nc - VIC-5 compliant NetCDF parameter files with values taken from the L2015 project for domain $DOMAIN (which is one of "CONUS_MX" or "USMX"). params.CONUS_MX.MOD_IGBP.mode.2000_2016.nc - VIC-5 compliant NetCDF parameter file over the CONUS_MX domain, with land cover fractions taken from the MODIS MCD12Q1.006 product and an annual cycle of land surface properties (LAI, Fcanopy, albedo) derived from the climatological mean of MODIS observations over the period 2000-2016. params.USMX.NLCD_INEGI.$LCID.2000_2016.nc - VIC-5 compliant NetCDF parameter file over the USMX domain, with land cover fractions taken from the NLCD_INEGI dataset, from year = $LCID, and an annual cycle of land surface properties (LAI, Fcanopy, albedo) derived from the climatological mean of MODIS observations over the period 2000-2016. params.USMX.NLCD_INEGI.$LCID.$YYYY_$YYYY.nc - VIC-5 compliant NetCDF parameter file over the USMX domain, with land cover fractions taken from the NLCD_INEGI dataset, from year = $LCID, and an annual cycle of land surface properties (LAI, Fcanopy, albedo) derived from the MODIS observations from a single year $YYYY. veg_hist.$DOMAIN.$LCTYPE.$LCID.2000_2016.nc - timeseries of monthly land surface properties (LAI, Fcanopy, albedo) from MODIS observations spanning years 2000-2016, over domain $DOMAIN, aggregated over land cover classification $LCTYPE from year $LCID.

title: Extended LamaH-CE: LArge-SaMple DAta for Hydrology and Environmental Sciences for Central Europe
description: Version 1.0: Please be aware that this version of the dataset is NOT the final revised one! The paper is currently still in progress. The Extended LamaH-CE dataset represents an enhanced version of the original LamaH-CE dataset (Klingler et al., 2021), providing comprehensive hydrometeorological time series and catchment attributes for 859 gauged basins in Central Europe. This extended version serves as supplementary material to the paper "BiasCast: Learning and adjusting real time biases from meteorological forecasts to enhance runoff predictions" and incorporates multiple state-of-the-art meteorological forcing datasets to enable advanced hydrological modeling and forecasting applications. Important Note: This Extended LamaH-CE dataset contains only the modified components. All enhancements were made exclusively to: A_basins_total_upstrm: Traditional catchment delineation (topographic catchments) D_gauges: Enhanced with qmin, qmax, and renamed qobs to qmean For all other components (aggregation levels B and C, catchment attributes, shapefiles, and documentation), users should refer to the original LamaH-CE dataset. Additional Meteorological Forcings The Extended LamaH-CE incorporates four major meteorological datasets, spatially aggregated to the catchment scale: E-OBS: High-resolution gridded observational dataset for European climate variables MSWEP: Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation with global coverage GLEAM: Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model for evapotranspiration and soil moisture ECMWF HRES: Deterministic forecasts from the Integrated Forecasting System All data sources are placed in the column headers as a prefix to the meteorological variable (e.g. ERA5L_2m_temp_mean). Enhanced Discharge Data The runoff time series have been augmented with additional statistical measures derived from hourly LamaH-CE: qmin: Daily minimum discharge qmax: Daily maximum discharge qmean: Daily mean discharge (renamed from qobs in the original version) Disclaimer The authors have processed this dataset with care and performed plausibility checks on all outputs. However, users acknowledge that neither the dataset creators nor the original data providers can be held liable for any errors, omissions, or consequences arising from the use of this dataset. Users are encouraged to perform their own quality assessments appropriate for their specific applications. License Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) This change from the original CC BY 4.0 license is necessitated by the inclusion of meteorological forcings with non-commercial restrictions. Acknowledgments We acknowledge the data providers for E-OBS (ECA&D project), MSWEP (GloH2O), GLEAM (Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model team), and ECMWF for making their datasets available. We further ask kindly for compliance in citing the data providers in the LamaH-CE paper.

title: AZ-Hydro — Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use: Software, Input Data, Models, Raster and Well Package Predictions, and Validation at 2 km Resolution (1896–2099)
description: AZ-Hydro: Historical and Projected Arizona Annual Water Use, 1896–2099 (v1.2) A 2 km-resolution gridded dataset of Arizona groundwater and surface-water withdrawals, irrigation consumptive use, and pumping-induced stream capture, spanning 204 years (1896–2099), with per-pixel uncertainty from a six-component framework and a well-level package for ~170,000 registered consumptive wells. Companion data archive for Majumdar et al. (submitted to Nature Scientific Data; preprint https://doi.org/10.31223/X56N63) and Majumdar et al. (in prep., AGU Earth’s Future). Version 1.2 (code release v1.2.0). See What’s new in v1.2 below. What’s in this deposit File Size Contents Audience az-hydro-headline.7z ~8.7 GB Self-contained subset of every key output: six-band augmented per-pixel, per-year withdrawal, consumptive-use, and stream capture rasters (prediction, σ, CV, SNR, lower and upper 95 % CI); the GeoParquet well package; per-basin and per-sub-basin time series; the CAP shortage-scenario sweep; era-mean and trend figures; validation and intercomparison outputs. Most users want this. Reviewers and downstream users of the published product az-hydro-data.7z ~80 GB Full reproducibility archive (~220 GB uncompressed): everything in the headline archive plus the raw inputs, cross-validation outputs, intermediate input stacks, and per-component uncertainty rasters (σ_MACA, σ_model, σ_irr, σ_LULC, σ_GW, σ_USBR, σ_CU). Anyone re-running the pipeline from scratch az-hydro-1.2.0.zip ~64 MB Tagged source-code release (Python pipeline, GEE export and upload scripts, documentation), identical to the GitHub repository at tag v1.2.0. Anyone running the pipeline README.md, HEADLINE_README.md, ADWR_readme.txt ~50 KB Current copies of the guides inside the archives: Data/README.md (full archive), Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive), and the ADWR folder’s readme.txt. They supersede the copies inside the .7z files, which predate the final author list and citations. Everyone Inside each .7z, Data/HEADLINE_README.md (headline archive) or Data/README.md (full archive) gives the per-directory inventory and the external-source citations. The standalone copies of these files in this deposit are the current versions. How to unpack the .7z files The archives use LZMA2 with solid-block compression, which macOS Archive Utility cannot open. Use one of: macOS: Keka or The Unarchiver Windows: 7-Zip, WinRAR, or Bandizip Linux: p7zip (for example apt install p7zip-full, then 7z x az-hydro-data.7z) What’s new in v1.2 Post-2026 Colorado River shortage. The central projection now uses the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines (U.S. Department of the Interior, August 2026), which reduce Arizona’s Colorado River apportionment by 760 kAF yr⁻¹ (CAP delivery factor 0.49, groundwater boost 7.5). The guidelines cover 2027–2028; 2029–2099 hold that latest official condition as a stand-in for continued shortage, not as a forecast. v1.0–v1.1 held the Tier 1 cut (512 kAF yr⁻¹) through 2099. Projected 2027–2099 groundwater withdrawal is 5.5 % higher and surface-water withdrawal 5.5 % lower than in v1.1; total withdrawal and all 1896–2026 predictions are unchanged. CAP scenario sweep. A ninth scenario applies the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines: 652 kAF yr⁻¹ of CAP delivery, the 900 kAF yr⁻¹ post-Tier baseline less the 248 kAF yr⁻¹ by which the guidelines’ 760 kAF yr⁻¹ Arizona reduction exceeds the Tier 1 cut that baseline is taken to include. It adds 1.30 MAF of groundwater pumping over 2027–2060 and 3.15 MAF over 2027–2099. The other scenarios are unchanged. Uncertainty ensemble. The ensemble members now apply the same dynamic CAP caps and floors as the central partition (a missing import had disabled them). σ for the groundwater and surface-water categories changes in every year; σ for total withdrawal does not. The scenario sweep keeps its full-delivery counterfactual. ADWR partner CSVs (Outputs/.../ADWR/). In v1.1, 14 of the 16 CSVs listed every basin-year twice, because the export also picked up the all-basin aggregate files. Each row now appears once, and Total_Predicted is built from the same per-basin series as the other categories, so Total_GW + Total_SW = Total_Predicted holds row by row. Basin totals count boundary pixels in every basin they touch, so summing basins exceeds the statewide total by about 2–3 %; statewide totals are in Annual_Summaries/. Headline archive now also includes the out-of-distribution probability rasters (OOD_Rasters/, 68 MB). GEE assets for the AZ-Hydro Explorer moved to projects/azhydro/assets/az-wu-v1-2/. Methods overview AZ-Hydro is a physics-constrained machine learning pipeline: XGBRF prediction of total annual withdrawal depth per 2 km pixel, trained on ADWR metered pumping records (1984–2024) with 22 predictors (actual and reference ET, precipitation, effective precipitation, temperature, land-cover fractions and densities, irrigated and groundwater-irrigation fractions, soil properties, water-table depth, well, surface-water-rights and canal densities, watershed streamflow, and pixel coordinates). Climate, ET, and land-cover inputs from different eras are joined into continuous 1896–2099 series by overlap-period bias correction. Density-ratio partition of the total into irrigation and non-irrigation withdrawals from groundwater and surface water, with consumptive use derived as CU = irrigation efficiency × irrigation withdrawal. The few free partition parameters were tuned to statewide USGS and ADWR records (USGS OFR 94-476, 1915–1990; USGS Circulars, 1950–2015; ADWR Annual Report totals and the 2019 ADWR shares); the machine learning totals are never adjusted. Six-component uncertainty quantification: σ_MACA (5 GCMs), σ_model (10 XGBRF seeds), σ_irr (irrigated-area input), σ_LULC (4 USGS land-use scenarios), σ_GW (5 recent well-registry snapshots), and σ_USBR (5 Upper Colorado River streamflow members), combined in quadrature and propagated to consumptive use (σ_CU). Stream capture index combining connectivity (exponential decay with water-table depth) and nearby surface-water availability, with pumping and connectivity uncertainty propagated to the capture volumes. Key validations Statewide agency reconciliation (calibration adequacy, not an independent test): 2017 ADWR total withdrawal 6.81 vs 7.00 MAF (−2.7 %); 2015 USGS groundwater withdrawal 2.96 vs 3.09 MAF (−4.1 %); 2019 ADWR irrigation share 74.2 % vs 72 %; 1955 and 1980 pumping peaks under-predicted by 6–11 %, with every reported total inside the model’s 95 % σ_total interval. Independent comparisons against USGS NHM withdrawals and consumptive use, USGS Reitz irrigation rasters, the USGS public-supply reanalysis, and CAP and SRP delivery records (statewide surface water within 0.8 % of the 1985–2024 CAP + SRP mean). WestWater Research (2026) CAP shortage anchor: Basic Coordination cumulative additional groundwater pumping 7.24 MAF over 2027–2060 vs 8.0 MAF (−9.5 %); Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF vs 8.7 MAF (the gap reflects AZ-Hydro’s no-regulatory-ceiling framing). CAP delivery shortage scenario sweep Nine scenarios (the no-cut Baseline_900kAF; DCP Tiers 0, 1, 2a, 2b, and 3; the 2027–2028 Operating Guidelines; WestWater Basic Coordination; Extreme Shortage) re-partitioned over 2026–2099. Cumulative additional groundwater pumping over 2027–2060: Operating Guidelines 1.30 MAF, DCP Tier 1 4.05 MAF, DCP Tier 3 10.69 MAF, Basic Coordination 7.24 MAF, Extreme Shortage 13.08 MAF. Basin and per-pixel maps, cumulative σ, and signal-to-noise figures are included for the 2027–2060 and 2027–2099 windows. External datasets required to reproduce the pipeline (not redistributed here) The pipeline reads four USGS ScienceBase data products that must be downloaded separately: USGS NHM withdrawals (Haynes et al. 2023): irrigation withdrawals and efficiency by HUC12, 2000–2020 USGS NHM consumptive use reanalysis (Martin et al. 2023; Martin et al. 2025): irrigation consumptive use by HUC12 USGS public-supply reanalysis (Luukkonen et al. 2023; Alzraiee et al. 2024): public-supply withdrawals by HUC12 USGS Reitz historical ET (Reitz et al. 2023; Reitz, Sanford & Saxe 2023): 800 m gridded ET Bundled here directly: ADWR Well Registry and metered pumping records, GW basin / AMA-INA / CAP / SRP / streamflow / USBR vectors, HarDWR water rights (Lisk et al. 2024), GRAIN canal network (Suresh et al. 2026), and the Ma et al. (2026) water-table depth. See Data/README.md inside each .7z for the exact file names and folders. title: HYD-RESPONSES: High-resolution daily catchment-level time series for relevant hydro-meteorological variables, (water) deficit accumulation and streamflow droughts for Switzerland
description: Data Description: The HYD-RESPONSES dataset provides daily catchment-level time-series for key hydro-meteorological variables (including precipitation, snow water equivalent, temperature, soil moisture, evaporation and streamflow). The data set covers 184 small to large FOEN-catchments in Switzerland. The catchments range across a variety of streamflow regime types, mean altitudes, biogeographic regions and anthropogenic influences. The time series data was aggregated from high-resolution spatially gridded products provided by MeteoSwiss (RhiresD, TabsD, TmaxD, TminD, SrelD), MeteoSwiss and the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research (SLF) (SPASS), SLF (OSHD) and ECMWF (ERA5-LAND). Daily average streamflow measurement series were provided by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN). Indicators related to snowfall, snowmelt and (potential) water balance were derived. The dataset further provides three standardized drought indices (SPI, SPEI, SMRI) for multiple aggregation-scales from 1 to 24 months (mostly in 3-monthly steps). Additional indicators of accumulated water deficits are provided by time series of cumulative deficits for both (potential) water balance and streamflow. For all variables and indices, the climatology and the (standardized) anomalies are available at various time scales (daily, monthly, seasonal, and yearly). Drought event time series are provided for both variable and fixed threshold definitions and are accompanied by characteristics on event duration. Detailed catchment descriptors were also extracted from various input products and are provided for all catchments. Data Organization: - Dataset provided as .zip-File - Data files are provided in .csv-Format (semi-colon separator) - The README.txt provides a detailed documentation of folders, data structure, variables and file-naming conventions. - Catchment outlets and outlines are provided as ESRI shapefiles (.shp) - Code examples are provided Folder structure: code_examples data ├── 01_timeseries │ ├── 00_meta_information │ ├── 01_base_variables │ ├── 02_derived_variables │ ├── 03_anomalies │ │ └── zscores │ ├── 04_standardized_indices │ │ ├── SMRI │ │ ├── SPEI │ │ └── SPI │ ├── 05_cumulative_deficits │ └── 06_events_nrs │ ├── cumulative_deficits │ └── hydrological_events ├── 02_climatology │ ├── 00_meta_information │ ├── 01_regular │ └── 02_DOY_movingwindow └── 03_descriptive Further reading & methodological details: Copernicus ESSD journal data paper [preprint]: von Matt, C., Stocker, B., and Martius, O.: HYD-RESPONSES: daily hydro-meteorological catchment-level time series to analyse HYDrological drought dynamics in RESPONSE to (cumulative) water deficits in Swiss catchments, Earth Syst. Sci. Data Discuss. [preprint], https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2025-383, in review, 2025. Code Examples (Tutorial): A tutorial demonstrating the handling and use of the HYD-RESPONSES dataset can be found at: https://github.com/codicolus/HYD-RESPONSES Funding: The HYD-RESPONSES project was funded by the Swiss Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).

title: Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland
description: Main data and methods used for Roberts et al. (2026) - "Assessing upper bounds for solar-powered Controlled Environment Agriculture on existing cropland" Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 10:1945186 Methods - CEA energy demand model setup To compare CEA powered by PV with crop-specific production globally, we derived a spatially-explicit energy demand per CEA. This type of comparison has been addressed in localized contexts in Weidner et al.[19], but lack a global scope as indicated in Bomford[23], Righini et al.[24,37], and Stanghellini & Katzin[27]. While there are many different greenhouse production models available[38], the specific aim of this study was to examine CEA systems and energy use on a global scale and this led to the construction of a model to address this aim. We developed a simple mechanistic model similar to the Van Henten model[39,40] as a way of incorporating experimental CEA crop production values and parameters[24] across a global spatial array (Supplementary Fig. 2). In order to make the model globally applicable, we made certain elements more generalized than they might be in a site-specific model, such as the building design, crop growing parameters and production system, building interaction with outside conditions, and the indoor environment control systems. The CEA yields, harvest metrics, and light requirements were taken directly from Righini et al.[24]. In that study, the authors compiled and analysed CEA metrics across multiple studies as well as their own experiments for wheat[28–30], soybean[24], potato[28,31,32], and tomato[24]. CEA aims to homogenize crop outputs and yields regardless of the geographic location, seasons, and local growing conditions. We applied this assumption to our model and kept CEA yields constant for each crop across the global spatial array. The yields from individual studies in Righini et al.[24] were analysed for parameters such as light requirements (photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD)), the growing cycle length (days), and the resulting yields in terms of plant density, harvest index (ratio of harvested biomass to total plant biomass), fresh harvest yield per growing cycle, dry harvest yield per cycle, and annual fresh weight yield (as the sum of multiple growing cycles possible per year). The values from that study used in this CEA energy model are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Long-term and continuous datasets on CEA for different crops such as those included in this study were not available. Hence, we extrapolated from the experimental results that were available to assume multiple yields per year (3-4) that would be possible given the reported growing production times and days to harvest. The reference experimental studies all used soilless growing set-ups (e.g., hydroponic), so the same is assumed in our modelled CEA. Mills[34] also compared energy demands across CEA studies and found differences between and across crop types. Mills[34] acknowledges that for crops such as wheat, few studies are available and in some cases, there is a reliance on modelled crop simulations. Given the discrepancies and potentially large ranges between crops and individual studies, we chose to directly apply the RIghini et al. CEA data compilation as the main source of crop specific parameters. Two types of CEA were evaluated, a high-tech closed greenhouse (GH) and a vertical farm (VF), to model the energy required for each set-up to achieve the target yields as compiled in Righini et al.[24]. The mechanistic greenhouse model assumed uniform internal conditions, also known as a “perfectly stirred tank”[39], and considered water vapour and energy balances in a similar way to the Van Henten model[38–40] (Supplementary Tables 1 & 3). We adapted the basic greenhouse balance equations for energy and water vapour from the van Henten model[39,40] to run the simplified model on global scales to calculate the CEA energy demand: dE/dt = QSun + QHeat + QLamp - QVent - QLatent - QCon – QFIR – Qcool (J m-2 s-1 = W m-2) dMW/dt = WTrans + WEvap + WHum - WCond - WVent - WDehum (kg {water vapor} m-2 s-1) dE/dt = net change of energy Q = rate of heat transfer from the various factors, inside and outside the growing space dMW/dt = net change of water mass W = rate of water vapor change over time from inside and outside factors More detailed processes can be captured in van Henten[39,40] or other greenhouse models[38]; however, to represent the major drivers of energy use, we only focused on these specific aspects. The process for calculating the influence of solar radiation was the same for both GH and VF and was an adapted version of the equation[24]: Energy Uselights = PPFD * photoperiod * 3600 * ηlights *10-6 (MJ m-2 day-1) ηlights= electrical efficacy The walls in the VF had 0% light entering, whereas the GH had 82% of solar radiation entering the growing space[22]. For incoming solar radiation, the daily total values were per month for an average daily solar radiation (J m-2 day-1). This incoming average daily solar radiation load was converted to a PPFD (μmol m-2 s-1) as the total daily PPFD or Daily Light Interval (DLI) as mol m-2 day-1. The PPFD and photoperiod for each crop from Righini et al.[24] was converted into a DLI requirement per day. The difference between the actual DLI and this required DLI indicated the lighting (J m-2 day-1) shortfall. Dividing this shortfall by the electrical efficacy*16 of the lights gave the average daily supplemental lighting demand (MJ m-2 day-1) for each month of 2020. While there are other potential processes or factors that would contribute to CEA energy demand, such as water pumps and irrigation, mechanized automation, and computer and sensor controls, these are relatively minor compared to the major energy drivers such as supplemental lighting, growing space heating and cooling, and ventilation[24]. Between the two CEA set-ups, there were minor adjustments to the building dimensions, crop growing area, and wall insulation properties. The simplified building designs similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] were intended to capture the basic parameters of the indoor growing space and basic interactions with the outdoor environment. In this way, the major drivers of CEA energy demand could be compared while avoiding specific building designs that vary by specific location and use. In this simulation, the vertical farm and closed greenhouse each had supplemental lighting, temperature, and humidity controls to maintain the same light requirements, indoor conditions, and annual yields depending on the crop requirements. The model considered a 1 ha GH (75% of the building footprint is considered usable as growing area) and a 0.25 ha VF (with 4 stacked layers that utilize 75% of the building footprint for growing area). The VF yield was assumed to be four times per hectare of building footprint compared to the GH as a way to capture the increased production capacity potential for the VF. Additionally, the VF was assumed to be 8m in height and the GH was assumed to be 4m in height. The same indoor environment was assumed for both systems and in turn the capacity to maintain that growing space environment is what drives the energy demand (Supplementary Table 1 & 3). We used the average daily light (PPFD) requirements, photoperiod, and annual yields according to Righini et al.[24] and included updated lighting and indoor environmental parameters to meet the best available standards for LEDs and heat pumps (Supplementary Table 4). The values presented by Righini et al.[24] include their own data for tomato and soybean experiments as well as a compilation of previous experiments for wheat[28–30] and potato[28,31,32] trials. Each of the selected experiments may have differed in specific CEA designs; however, all were soilless systems that relied entirely on supplemental lighting for crop growth. The mechanistic greenhouse model had a time-step of one day for all indoor processes. The outdoor climate conditions were averaged for each month and recorded as the average daily temperature, relative humidity, and solar radiation flux for each grid cell per month. The model received the daily average (for each month) as input data and first calculated the influence of the outside factors on the indoor growing parameters (temperature, relative humidity, and light) for both VF and GH. Then for each growing space parameter, the corresponding CEA component was forced to correct the factor to bring it back into the target range. For heating and cooling this was done with a heat pump, for relative humidity with humidifier or ventilation, and LEDs for supplemental lighting. The energy requirement for each component to maintain the target growing conditions was summed for each average day per month. These daily energy totals were multiplied by the number of days per month to return a monthly energy demand based on the average day in that month. These monthly values were then summed to return an annual energy demand. This annual energy demand was divided by the annual CEA yield per building to give the energy use efficiency (MJ kg-1) for each crop and CEA system. The resulting energy demand reflects the energy needed to maintain those constant internal conditions within the target ranges. By doing this, we were able to compare the plant specific growing parameters and yields from Righini et al.[24] between VF and GH systems. CEA energy demand simulation inputs The selected crops for the study were wheat, potato, soybean, and tomato to represent grain, legume, tuber, and vegetable crop types. The temperature control (15-23°C) and relative humidity range (60-85%) were set at levels similar to Weidner et al.[19,41] (Supplementary Table 3) We assumed a fixed biomass production per growing cycle and year (yield biomass per m2 and harvest index adapted from Righini et al.[24] instead of simulating crop growth over time and across growth stages. Because evapotranspiration is a complex process that varies between crops and plant stages, we applied a single generalised evapotranspiration rate of 4.5 mm day-1 for all crops[42–44]. Additionally, the energy to power water pumps and recirculation is relatively insignificant compared to other CEA processes and the water use itself might be over 90% lower (for both closed greenhouses and vertical farms) than comparable field systems[20,24,45]. For this reason, water use and energy for the irrigation and water pump and recirculation system were not included. A heat pump is used to maintain the internal temperature within the target range with a Coefficient of Performance, for heating, (COP) of 4.0 and an Energy Efficiency Ratio, for cooling, (EER) of 13.0[46]. These COP and EER are general values in order to reflect that these efficiencies could be influenced by local conditions and product designs. The building wall insulation R-value was kept at 3 for the GH[47] and 15 for the VF[48]. Supplemental lighting from LEDs was set to 3.5 mmol J-1 to represent the current best available standard[22,27] (Supplementary Table 4). ERA 5 Agrometeorological environmental data[49] (0.1° x 0.1° resolution) were used for daily measurements for solar radiation flux (J m-2), temperature (K at 2m height), and relative humidity (% at 2m height at 12h) for the year 2020. The daily values for each grid cell were averaged for each month in the year 2020. This averaged daily value per month for the climate parameters (solar radiation, temperature, relative humidity) were input into the CEA energy demand model at 1-day time steps. The use of a monthly averaged value for each climate factor was a trade-off to run the model efficiently on a global array while still capturing site and seasonal variations. The model outputs were calculated in total energy demand (MJ) per day and then summed for a monthly and annual total. The annual energy demand to crop yield (MJ kg-1) or energy use efficiency in each CEA system was then calculated per grid cell. Both monthly energy demand and annual energy use efficiency were downscaled to a 1km grid in order to compare to the higher resolution land use and solar PV potential model outputs. The resulting energy use efficiency as MJ kg-1 for each crop calculated by region for both CEA systems is shown in Fig. 2. Global crop area, yield, and production We used a data harmonisation approach based on the HILDA+ land use reconstruction model[2], to allocate 2020 crop production (t km-2) and crop harvest area (ha km-2) for the target crops to a 1km global grid array. This approach allowed us to harmonise the outputs of multiple crop models, datasets, and statistical inventories to produce crop area, yield, and production maps for each target crop. In HILDA+, the cropland areas were isolated and used to mask the CROPGRIDS crop-specific crop area data (reference year 2020)[36]. GAEZ v4 (reference year 2015)[35], along with the statistical data for FAO country level harvest area and production quantity totals (reference year 2020)[50] were used to assign the pixel-level harvest area (ha) and yields (t/ha) for the target crops. This was done by first normalizing the GAEZ v4 crop yield values, i.e. dividing them by their national and cropland-wide mean, as well as normalizing the CROPGRIDS crop area values by their national and cropland-wide sum (all constrained by HILDA+ cropland and at least 5% CROPGRIDS crop coverage). This normalization was done in order to align each input dataset with the same consistent spatial array and projection. The normalized values, crop yield and area, were then multiplied by FAO crop yield and harvested area in 2020, respectively. The crop production (t) was finally derived by a pixel-based multiplication of country- and crop-specific yield (t ha-1) and harvested areas (ha). Each crop then had a specific harvest area (ha), yield (t ha-1), and production (t) per grid cell for the year 2020. In order to harmonise these different datasets, steps were taken to minimise inter-dataset variability. FAO statistics only report crop area harvested, which could include multiple harvests on the same area, so the CROPGRIDS crop cultivation area layer was used to set a fraction of crop area per grid cell prior to allocating the FAO area harvested within each country’s grid cells. Upper thresholds for crop area were set to limit any instance where the area from multiple harvests were applied to the same grid cell. In this way we were able to remove inconsistencies or data artifacts that would otherwise inflate the crop area beyond what was available in the grid cell (i.e., more than 100 ha crop area for a 100 ha grid cell). The data harmonisation process of crop area, yield, and production is simplified in Supplementary Fig. 4. PV-powered CEA comparison with 2020 crop area, yield, and production The CEA crop yields[24] were kept constant across the global array in order to test the area and PV energy capacity to scale these experimental values globally. The multiple datasets[35,36,50] used across the analysis reported the reference yields and production in harvested biomass. For this reason, we used CEA production and yield values for harvested biomass. For different research questions, this metric could be changed to dry harvest weight, calories, or other specific nutritional or agronomic units. The first step to calculate the comparison against 2020 crop production was to determine the CEA building area needed to meet 2020 production (t km-2) per grid cell. The annual CEA yields were calculated per growing area and were set per grid cell to reflect the CEA systems (0.75ha growing area per 1ha GH building area and 0.75ha growing area per 0.25ha VF building area). The 2020 production array was divided by the annual CEA yield (per growing area) per crop to give the CEA building area needed for year-round CEA production in each grid cell. This CEA footprint requirement was summed per hectare for GH or per 0.25 hectare for VF per grid cell. To calculate the solar PV area needed for the CEA, the monthly solar PV potential (kWh m-2) was derived from Saxena et al.[33]. The area available for PV per grid cell was calculated as the harvest area subtracted by the CEA building area per grid cell. The surface area coverage of the solar PV was assumed to be 75% of a given area[22], so the potential energy available to the CEA was reduced by this factor. This PV potential was then multiplied by an efficiency factor[51] (26.8%) for conversion to usable electricity. The total CEA energy demand per building (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) per grid cell was multiplied by the CEA building area requirement to calculate the total CEA energy demand per grid cell. The monthly PV area requirement to directly power the CEA was calculated by multiplying the potential PV energy by the CEA energy demand per grid cell. The process is summarized visually in Supplementary Fig. 3 and all CEA component inputs are summarized in Supplementary Tables 1-4. For year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for each grid cell became the fixed PV area needed to power the required CEA area for that grid cell. No energy storage was assumed from one day to the next, so each day had only the monthly 1-day average to fulfil the CEA demand. We also analysed continuous 9-month CEA production capacity as a way to reduce the energy demand and the required PV area to power the CEA. The reduction in yield capacity was taken into account and the CEA area needed to meet 2020-Production per grid cell was re-calculated. For the shortened 9-month production cycle, the 9-month stretch with the lowest PV area requirements to meet indoor energy demands were calculated per grid cell. Similar to the year-round production, the month with the greatest PV area requirement for this 9-month cycle, determined the PV area needed for that grid cell. The resulting area (ha) of PV needed to power a year-round or 9-month CEA is displayed spatially in Supplementary Fig. 7. This CEA building area plus PV area was the total area that was then compared to the crop harvest area per grid cell. The land area requirement balance (ha) was calculated by subtracting the CEA building footprint plus PV area from the crop area per grid cell. If the area balance was negative, then not enough area was available for the CEA-PV to meet 2020 production in that grid cell. If the balance was zero or positive, the CEA-PV matched 2020 production and any positive value could be considered a lower required land area than 2020 production area in ha. Only the grid cells with a positive area balance were used to calculate the potential extra or surplus production by allowing the model to utilise all crop area available and CEA production above 2020 production values. This extra-production was calculated by incrementally adding CEA units (1ha for GH and 0.25ha for VF) and the required PV area per building. This process was done iteratively until the crop harvest area in that grid cell reached zero. The sum of this extra production according to the CEA building area added, was then added to that grid cell total production quantity. The spatial distribution of areas where CEA met 2020 production can be seen in Fig. 3. The global totals and comparison between CEA systems for harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production, production quantity (t) met by CEA, lower CEA-PV land area requirements compared to 2020 production (ha), and extra production (t) by CEA are given in Fig. 4. The regional breakdowns relative to the global totals as well as the breakdown within each region are given in Supplementary Figs. 8&9. Yield gap analysis The yield gap analysis and comparison were done to apply a single metric for comparing crop production challenges globally. For this study we used the GAEZ v4 crop-wise Yield Achievement Ratio[35] (YAR) global gridded (5 arc minutes) dataset for the most recent average (2009-2011). The YAR was calculated by GAEZ as the ratio of actual (average) yields to the attainable yields for each grid cell. The attainable yields were calculated as the biophysical influences (e.g., solar radiation, water, nutrients, temperature) on yield (potential yield) while considering location specific constraints (e.g., soil or terrain, pest pressure, management). For the crops analysed in this study, GAEZ only has YAR data for wheat, soybean, and potato, so we limited the yield gap analysis to these crops. The ratio of actual/ attainable yields is inversely proportional to the yield gap, as a higher ratio indicates a smaller yield gap. We used the GAEZ YAR data that had already been divided into bins corresponding to the crop-wise YAR. The 2020 crop-wise harvest area (ha) was compared to the corresponding YAR to calculate the distribution of crop harvest area per YAR bin. This distribution (percent of harvest area (ha)) per YAR bin was plotted to complement the global YAR maps plotted directly from the GAEZ dataset. CEA-PV system performance compared to 2020 production was then evaluated against the reference crop yield gaps. Only grid cells where there was spatial agreement between the CROPGRIDS and GAEZ YAR datasets were considered. To analyse CEA-PV relationships with crop yield gaps, only the grid cells where CEA-PV demonstrated the ability to meet 2020 production were considered. Including only these CEA-PV net area positive areas was done to focus on the technical potential of CEA in alleviating yield gap constraints. In our analysis, CEA-PV net negative could not meet the same production values as 2020 production without additional crop area, it was assumed that CEA in these areas would be able to aid in yield gap closures. The area (ha) that was net positive CEA-PV crop area was summed for each YAR bin and the percent of the net positive CEA-PV crop area was plotted alongside the total crop harvest area distribution. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides a general overview of the yield gap analysis process. Electricity grid constraints The Arderne et al.[52] electrical grid dataset was used to evaluate the current electrical grid coverage in areas that overlap with areas that meet 2020 production (CEA-PV technical capacity areas). Where there was at least medium-voltage electricity, a 2km buffer was set as the maximum distance for connection to these electricity grids. The grid cells where there was overlap of this grid network and buffer with these CEA-PV grid cells that met 2020 production were summed, as well as those that were outside of this 2km buffer. The grid cells were then multiplied by the crop harvest area (ha) in that grid cell and then summed crop at the country- and regional-levels. The proportion of harvest area (ha) where CEA met 2020 production within the 2km electricity grid was then calculated for country and region as seen in Fig. 5. The spatial overlap of areas where CEA met 2020 production and the electricity grid can be seen in Supplementary Fig. 10. Aridity Index The Global Aridity Index Database as described in Zomer et al.(52) was used to compare where CEA matched 2020 production against aridity zones. The aridity index was divided into bins according to the index value. These index values were overlaid on the grid cells where CEA matched 2020 production. The harvest area (ha) was then multiplied by the number of grid cells within each index bin. The harvest area (ha) where CEA matched 2020 production was plotted according to the aridity index bin and results are given in Supplementary Fig. 11. Model assumption sensitivity A deterministic sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate CEA-PV equivalent capacity reactions to changes in model assumptions. The sensitivity analysis evaluated changing assumptions around three parameters directly influencing CEA-PV area requirements and subsequent equivalent-capacity calculations: CEA crop yield, CEA energy demand, and PV conversion efficiency. Changes to each assumption were considered individually and for their combined effects on CEA-PV equivalent capacity. The main “baseline” analysis for GH and VF applied the experimental CEA yields described above and calculated the CEA building area required to match 2020 crop production in each grid cell, while the PV area requirement was determined from the corresponding CEA energy demand and a baseline PV conversion efficiency of 26.8%. For the yield sensitivity analysis, the annual CEA yield for each crop was reduced by 10%, 25%, and 50%. The required CEA building area was then recalculated directly from 2020 crop production using the reduced yield while retaining the same GH- or VF-specific growing areas and corresponding year-round or 9-month growing cycles. The greater CEA area required under lower yields also increased growing area and associated PV area requirements to match 2020 crop production. For the energy sensitivity, CEA energy demand per unit growing area was increased by 10%, 25%, and 50%, while CEA yields and building area requirements were maintained at baseline input values. In turn, the corresponding PV area requirement increased to meet the increased energy demand. For the PV efficiency sensitivity, conversion efficiency was reduced from the baseline input value of 26.8% to 22%, while CEA crop yields and energy demands were kept constant. The PV area requirements were then required to provide the same amount of energy to meet CEA energy demands. Additionally, the joint effects of combining CEA yield reductions, energy demand increases, and PV conversion efficiency reductions were evaluated. For each joint effect scenario, the revised CEA building area and PV requirements were compared to the available crop-wise harvested area in each grid cell using the same approach as the baseline analysis to calculate equivalent capacity. The sensitivity analysis tested the change in absolute area (ha), production (t), and less crop area required (ha) and corresponding global percentages for the CEA systems, year-round and 9-month growing cycles, and four crops. The sensitivity analysis therefore tested how these CEA systems performed under less favourable model assumptions rather than representing probabilistic uncertainty ranges. title: Global Trends in Hydroclimatic Variables (1979–2023) from ERA5 at 0.25° Resolution
description: This dataset provides global gridded trend estimates (Z-values) for key hydroclimatic variables over the period 1979–2023, derived from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset. The analysis was performed to detect long-term changes in climate and water cycle drivers at a spatial resolution of 0.25° (~25 km). Variables included (all in .mat format): Z_air_temperature.mat – near-surface at 2m air temperature trends Z_cloud_cover.mat – total cloud cover trends Z_ETo.mat – reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith) trends Z_long_radiation.mat – net longwave radiation trends Z_net_radiation.mat – net radiation trends Z_PET.mat – potential evapotranspiration (Priestley–Taylor) trends Z_precipitation.mat – total precipitation trends Z_short_radiation.mat – net shortwave radiation trends Z_soil_moisture.mat – volumetric soil moisture trends Z_soil_temperature.mat – soil temperature trends Z_solar_radiation.mat – incoming solar radiation trends Z_VPD.mat – vapor pressure deficit trends Z_wind_speed.mat – near-surface at 2m wind speed trends Methodology: Long-term trends were calculated using the Mann-Kendall test for trend detection. Significance levels were evaluated at α = 0.05. Trend magnitudes are expressed as Z-values (normalized test statistics). Spatial and Temporal Coverage: Time span: 1979–2023 (45 years) Spatial resolution: 0.25° × 0.25° global grid Dataset source: ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF) Applications: This dataset can be used for: Hydroclimatic and environmental change assessments Attribution studies on drivers of evaporative demand and water cycle intensification Regional and global climate modeling validation Agricultural and hydrological impact studies File format: All files are provided as MATLAB .mat files containing 2D gridded arrays corresponding to the global extent. Note: All figures presented in the dataset description can be reproduced using the accompanying MATLAB script plot_global_trends_ERA5_Zmaps.m, which loads the .mat files and generates the global Z-value maps for each variable. title: Lund University Global Drought Dataset (LUGD), 1981–2025: Weekly 0.1° SPEI with Accumulation Timescales from 1 Week to 48 Months – Southern Hemisphere
description: The SPEI was calculated for 12 accumulation timescales ranging from 1 week to 48 months. The temporal index represents a pseudo-weekly time step, defined as four time steps per month starting on the 1st, 9th, 16th, and 23rd day of each month. Daily precipitation (P) was obtained from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation dataset (MSWEP V2), which combines rain-gauge observations, satellite retrievals, and atmospheric reanalysis products to produce globally gridded precipitation estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution from 1979 to 2025. Daily potential evapotranspiration (PET) was obtained from the Bristol global PET dataset, which provides global PET estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution for the period 1981–2025. Bristol PET is calculated using the FAO Penman–Monteith formulation based on meteorological variables from ERA5-Land. The climatic water balance was first calculated as D=P−PET, for accumulation timescales of 1 week, 2 weeks, and 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 48 months, capturing drought variability from short-term events to multi-year conditions. The accumulated water balance series was then fitted to a three-parameter log-logistic distribution and transformed to a standardized normal distribution N(0,1), i.e. SPEI, following the method of Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010).

The temporal index represents a pseudo-weekly time step, defined as four time steps per month starting on the 1st, 9th, 16th, and 23rd day of each month. Daily precipitation (P) was obtained from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation dataset (MSWEP V2), which combines rain-gauge observations, satellite retrievals, and atmospheric reanalysis products to produce globally gridded precipitation estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution from 1979 to 2025. Daily potential evapotranspiration (PET) was obtained from the Bristol global PET dataset, which provides global PET estimates at 0.1° spatial resolution for the period 1981–2025. Bristol PET is calculated using the FAO Penman–Monteith formulation based on meteorological variables from ERA5-Land. The climatic water balance was first calculated as D=P−PET, for accumulation timescales of 1 week, 2 weeks, and 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, and 48 months, capturing drought variability from short-term events to multi-year conditions. The accumulated water balance series was then fitted to a three-parameter log-logistic distribution and transformed to a standardized normal distribution N(0,1), i.e. SPEI, following the method of Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010).

title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height: Surface elevation wnd100m: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth: Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness: Surface roughness length influx_toa: Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo: Surface albedo temperature: Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature: Soil temperature at level 4 runoff: Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct: Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse: Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude: Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth: Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN. Source: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Terms of Use These cutouts contain processed meteorological data derived from ERA5, provided by the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), and SARAH-3, provided by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). Users must acknowledge EUMETSAT when using or redistributing the data and are requested to cite the original SARAH-3 dataset: https://doi.org/10.5676/EUM_SAF_CM/SARAH/V003 Licensing and Attribution The cutouts are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, subject to the attribution requirements associated with the original data sources. title: Earthen berm stochastic simulation (Landlab): code and data
description: Model code and simulation output for a global sensitivity study of earthen berms in dryland valleys. Each run is a 100-year Landlab simulation driven by CLIGEN storms for Tucson, Arizona, run once with a berm and once without it, using the same storms. The record contains the model (berm_driver.py) and the CLIGEN station file, end-of-run results and storm-by-storm series for a 1,152-run main ensemble, paired berm and no-berm storm records for 189 runs of an earlier per-storm ensemble, an older per-decile summary of 128 of those runs, the script that extracted the 189 runs from the raw output, and the raw output itself. README.md describes the files, and DATA_DICTIONARY.md describes every column.
